en: Having bowed to Naṭeśa, the teacher of all the traditions of the phonemes, Śrīkaṇṭha composes this Dhātukārikā,
which delights the young. (1)
For the sake of understanding the genders and meanings of words, [I consulted] the Amara-kośa by Amarasiṃha and the Dharmādhikārin composed by the illustrious Cakravartin Ayyaṅgārya. (2)

Having studied this *Śabdakārikā*, which provides an awakening to the various forms of nouns ending in case-terminations (*subanta*), those who likewise desire to understand verbal roots (*dhātu*) [should study it as well]. (3)
For the benefit of those who are weary because the ancient Dhātupāṭha is difficult to study, and for the complete satisfaction of children who request it out of curiosity; (4)

First, for those who wish to travel the path of poetry, the very list of verbal roots (dhātupāṭha) is presented today in its proper order through well-composed and easily understood verses (kārikā). ||5||
The wise are invited here to examine it; let them either censure me or praise me.
Herein are the ten classes of roots beginning with *bhū*, as well as the *kaṇḍvādī* roots. (6)
In this [work], there are roots that take the middle voice (ātmanepada) and likewise those that take the active voice (parasmaipada);
similarly, there are those belonging to both voices, as well as those with an indicatory letter *i* (seṭ), those without it (aniṭ), and all those with an indicatory *m* (mit).
The continuations and their connections, as well as the purposes of those respective effects, are being examined;
the exposition of the subject matter is difficult even for the son of Bhīma. 8.
It is clarified slightly according to the method of explanation used by the Easterners;
for even though there are sentences within the verse composed of words belonging to other verses. (9)
The rule that "there is no positive concomitance" is not observed anywhere. 10.

Nevertheless, even though poets have resorted to this restriction here and there in various places within their poetry for the sake of allaying the fatigue of those desiring to learn, [the following applies].
Because the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is also observed here by virtue of restatement, in certain cases there is a connection between the verses and the statements occurring therein. 12.
The discrepancy caused by the sequence of preceding and following [words] may be tolerated by those with sensitive hearts;
however, in that context, for the sake of avoiding doubt regarding the grammatical connection (anvaya), words such as "atha" at the end do not take the place of those at the beginning.
Thus this rule of Amarasimha has been adopted by me:
the root *bhū* is udātta when used in the sense of "existence" (*sattā*), whereas those roots marked with the anubandha *sa* are anudātta. (14)

The thirty-six roots beginning with *edh* are now described in order: *edh* is traditionally understood as "to increase"; *spardh*, however, is used in the sense of "rivalry" and is intransitive (akarmaka). ||15||
The desire to overcome another is here called *saṅgharṣa* (rivalry), because it is comprised solely by the meaning of the root of the verb for "another. (16)
The root *gādhṛ* is said to mean binding, establishing, and also desire;
*bādhṛ* means churning, and it is also designated as obstruction. (17)
The root *nāth* is said to be unaccented on its first syllable when used in the sense of begging, suffering, or seeking prosperity;
it is not so accented in the sense of protection. (18)
The root *dhā* is traditionally held to mean "holding" (*dhāraṇa*), while *skudi* is considered to mean "leaping up" (*utplavana*) and "lifting up" (*uddharaṇa*);
here, by the word "not sloping" (*apravaṇa*), leaping up and lifting up are intended. (19)
The root *śvid* is used in the sense of "to shine" (*śavaitya*) and is intransitive; *vad* is used in the sense of "praise" (*stuti*) and "salutation" (*abhivāda*);
*bhad* is used in the sense of "happiness" (*sukha*) and "welfare" (*kalyāṇa*); and *mad* is used in the sense of "joy" (*moda*), "intoxication" (*mada*), and "praise" (*stuti*). (20)
The roots *svap* and *ekānta* are used in the sense of "gone" (past); *spadi* is prescribed for slight movement, while *klid* is said to mean lamentation arising from grief. 21.
Therefore, it is declared to be transitive; *muda* is used in the sense of joy, *dada* in the sense of giving, *adas* in the sense of eating, and *ardā* in the sense of the act of tasting. (22)
The root *anubhū* is transitive; *ruc* has *svadi* as its object.
The roots *mān*, *krīḍana*, *urda*, *kurda*, *khurda*, and *gurda* [are used in the sense of measuring, playing, and so forth]. (23)
These four—guda, krīḍā, hāda, and ṣūda—are indeed recorded as being used only in the sense of play; ṣūda is used in the sense of trickling, while hāda is said to denote an indistinct sound. 24.
The root *hal* is recorded as meaning happiness; *avyakta-śabda* means indistinct sound; and *svāda* is known to mean tasting or relishing. ||25||
The root *pard* is used in the sense of making a sound; this *pard* is a sound like the rumbling of the bowels.
*Yat* is recorded in the sense of effort, and *yut* as well as *jut* are remembered in the sense of shining. (26)
The root *vidhṛ* is used in the sense of requesting; *śrathi* is said to mean looseness;
*grathi* denotes crookedness; and *kattha* is declared to mean boasting. (27)
Now, the verbal roots ending in the consonants of the thirty-eight *tavarga* class are declared here in their proper order as taking the *parasmaipada* (active voice) terminations. 28.
Therefore, in its movement toward that [state], it is called *saṃjñāna*;
in its pouring out, it is declared to be *cyuti*, and that is remembered as the act of moistening. ||29||
The suffix *aṅ* should be understood to apply in the sense of "slightness" (*iṣadartha*) as well as in the sense of "pervasion" (*abhivyāpti*).
This [root] *kṣar*, meaning "to flow," is also accepted by the wise even when deprived of the letter *y*. (30)

The root *manth* is used in the sense of churning; then there are *kuth*, *puth*, *luth*, and *math* in the sense of distressing; then *hiṃs* is used in the sense of injury; and finally, *ṣidh* is recorded in the sense of going. (31)
In the *Śāstra* and in auspicious contexts, the root *ṣidh* denotes "instruction"; *śāstra* is said to mean "teaching.
Then, *khādṛ* is taught in the sense of "eating," while *khad* would signify "firmness" and "injury. (32)
The root *bhakṣ* is intransitive in the sense of eating; then *bad* is said to mean steadiness;
*gad* means steadiness; *rad* is used for clear speech; and *rad* means scratching. (33)
*Vilekhana* means scratching; *bedana* means piercing. *Nada* is used for an indistinct sound.
*Arda* means going or begging; with the prefix *pra*, it means crying out (*gardati*). (34)
The root *tard* is used in the sense of violence; the word *karda* is desired in the sense of a contemptible sound.
For those who know it, the contemptible sound intended here is that of the belly (*kaukṣa*). 35.

The term *kharda* is declared to refer to the *daṃśūka* (the biting one), which consists of the acts of biting, harming, and so forth; however, here the word *daṃśūka* is used specifically for the activity of that biting one. (36)
If one desires supreme sovereignty, then [the mantra] "bandhane" is prescribed for the sake of binding. ||37||
The root *gaḍi* is said to mean "a swelling" (*gaḍu*) on a part of the body, specifically on one region of the face.

Regarding this, Kāśyapa maintains that these five roots beginning with *ati* do not have finite verbs (*tiṅ*) as their objects; however, others desire that they also take finite verbs as their objects. (38)
The root *ṇidi* is said to denote contempt, while *ṭunadi* is remembered to denote prosperity. ||39||
The root *cad* is said to mean "to delight," while *trad* is said to mean "motion.
Furthermore, *kad*, *krad*, and *klad* are said to signify both "calling out" and "weeping. (40)
*Paridevana* is declared [to mean] lamentation; *klid*, *śundh*, and *śuc* denote grieving.
Now, forty-two verbal roots are stated in their proper order. (41)
Those [roots] ending in a letter of the *ka*-group (velars) have an *anudātta* indicatory vowel (*anubandha*).
The root *śīkṛ* is used in the sense of "sprinkling," but this begins with a palatal (*tālavya*) letter; others [hold that it begins with a labial]. 42.
They say that *loka* begins with the dental [d]; in the sense of "seeing," *loka* is explained as such.
In the sense of "a collection," however, it is a *grantha*, or else it is the action of being strung together (*grathyamāna*). (43)

In the first [verse], the action of the stringer is desired; in the second, it would be intransitive; then in the third, it would be transitive; and in the fourth, the action of the stringer is one of exertion. 44.

In the context of sound, *utsāha* (exertion) is declared; likewise, *vṛddhi* is simply loftiness (*aunnatya*). Regarding doubt, *rekṛ* is fully taught, as are *sekṛ*, *srekṛ*, *sraki*, and *śraki*. (45)
In this context, three roots beginning with the dental *śak* are recorded as meaning "to go";
both those beginning with the palatal *śaṅk* are used in the sense of "doubt," and the root *śaki* is likewise said to express that same meaning. (46)
The root *ak* is used in the sense of a characteristic mark; *vaki* is used in the sense of crooked action;
*maki* is used in the sense of adorning and greed; and *kaka* denotes greed as well as fickleness. (47)
The root *garv* is said to mean pride; *vṛk* is used in the sense of seizing;
*cak* in the sense of satiety and resistance; and *kaṅgati* in the sense of motion. 48.
The roots *vaki*, *śvi*, *kri*, *ḍaukṛ*, *traukṛ*, *uṣkṛ*, *caṣkṛ*, and *vaskati*;
likewise *maskṛ*, *ṭīkṛ*, *ṭīkṛ*, *atikṛ*, *raghi*, and *laghi*. (49)
Some, however, declare that the third [root] here begins with the dental [d].
Laghi is used in the sense of ceasing from eating; āghi, vadhri, and maghi are three [others]. (50)
The "impelling of movement" (gatyākṣepa) is traditionally taught [as the function of *karman*], while "the impairment of memory" (smṛtyākṣepa) is proclaimed here [as the function of *kleśa*].
Others, however, say it is "in movement" (*gatau*) or "at the commencement of movement" (*gatyārambhe*), and that [the former] is the most excellent. (51)
In the sense of cheating or capability, some have recited the roots *drāghṛ*, *āghṛ*, and *lāghṛ*; others have even included the root *dhrāghṛ* in this very same list. 52.
The root *ā-yam* means "to lengthen"; *āyāma* is said to be length or extension.
From the root *ślāgh*, meaning "to praise," [the form *ślāghate* arises]; now follow the roots that take the *parasmaipada* (active voice) endings. (53)

The final letters of the *ka*-group (k, kh, g, gh, ṅ) are said to number fifty; they are used for downward movement, as well as for the terms *phakka* (a cripple), *ati* (excess), and *adhvaha* (a wayfarer) among the wicked in this world. 54.

The two [roots] *mand* and *gati* also denote moving slowly; they are said to signify a low state when used with the word *pada*. The root *tak* is used for vomiting, while *tak* is also said to mean a difficult life. 55.
The root *bukk* is used in the sense of barking; the barking of a dog (*svāna*) is called *bhaṣaṇa*.
However, the root *kakhati* here is said to be used in the sense of the act of laughing. (56)
The roots okhṛ, rākhṛ, lākhṛ, drākhṛ, and dhrākhṛ signify drying up; they also denote sufficiency. Furthermore, śākhṛ and ślākhṛ denote the action of pervading. 57.
Ukhokhī, vakhati, vakhir, makhamakhī, ṇakha, ṇakhīr, akharakhī, and likewise lakhalakhī, ikha. ||58||
Ikhiri-khirvalga, Ragī, Lagiścāgi-rvagirmagi, Tagis-tvagi-śragi, then Ślagi-cegī-rigirligi. (59)
In this [section], there are twenty-eight ending in *ga*, fifteen ending in *kha*, thirteen ending in *ga*, and others read four more ending in *stra*. 60.
The wise [know] *rikha*, *tra-khaṃ*, *trakhī*, and *śikhī* as well; they are also at the ends of vowels (*khānta*).
*Tvagi* occurs in the sense of trembling; furthermore, there are *yugi*, *jugi*, and *bagī*. (61)
The root *ghagh* is said to mean "avoiding," *maghi* means "laughing" and "adorned";
*śaṅghati* means "smelling. Now follow the roots ending in the final letters of the palatal class (*cavarga*). 62.
Indeed, twenty-one [roots] are said to have the anudātta accent as their indicatory mark (anubandha).
The root *varc* is declared to mean "to shine," while *ṣac* is said to mean "to sprinkle" and "to serve. (63)

The root *locṛ* is recorded as meaning "to see" or "speech"; *śacati* is remembered [as a root] in the sense of "to be able. *Śvac* and *śvacī* are said to mean "motion," while *kac* is used for the action of "binding. (64)
The roots *kac* and *kāc* are both said to mean "shining" and "binding.
The root *muc* occurs in the sense of "cleansing," while *dambha*, *śāṭhya*, and *kalkana* all signify "deceit. (65)
Others say that *vac* is used in the sense of speaking; however, it is intended [by some] in the senses of holding, honoring, heightening, and making manifest. (66)

The root *ṣṭuca* is used in the sense of propitiation; *ṛji* is used in the senses of going, standing, and also acquiring or earning; furthermore, *ṛji* and *bhṛjī* are used in the sense of the act of roasting or frying. (67)
Ejṛ, bhrējṛ, and bhrājṛ are used in the sense of shining; ījitṛ is used in the senses of motion and reproach.
These seventy-two roots ending in -vraj are declared to be parasmaipada (active-voice) verbs. ||68||

*Śuc* is used in the sense of grief; *kuc* in the sense of sound; *tārā* in the sense of crying out; *kruñcati* and *kuñcatī* signify crookedness and becoming small; *luñca* means removal; and *añcu* signifies movement. (69)
*Vañcu*, *cañcu*, and *tañcu* are used respectively for going and honoring;
*tvañcu*, *ruñcu*, and *lunñu* are also used in the sense of going—these eight, along with *mrucu* and *mlucu*, [are roots meaning "to go"]. (70)
The roots *grac*, *gluc*, *kuj*, and *khuj* are declared to be used in the sense of stealing;
*gluñc* and *ṣasj* are used in the sense of going, and *sajjati* is used in the middle voice (ātmanepada). 71.
The root *guj* is used in the sense of an indistinct sound; *arcati* is recorded in the sense of worship.
*Lmeccha* is said to denote an indistinct sound; it is also an incorrect word (*apaśabda*) when it is unclear. (72)
The term *lāch* is used in the sense of a mark (*lakṣaṇa*) or desire (*icchā*); *āchi* is used in the sense of extension (*āyāma*), while *hī* is said to denote shame (*lajjā*). (73)
The root *hurch* is said to mean crookedness; crookedness is the act of crawling away.
Maitreya says that *mūrch* means swelling and also delusion. (74)
The root *sphurch* is used in the sense of expansion; *yucch* and *ṛ* denote negligence; and *uch* denotes gathering.
*Uñcha* refers to the picking up of grains individually, while *sila* refers to the gathering of ears of grain and the like. (75)
Thus, according to the authority of the Yādavakośa, "uñcha" means "gleaning"; the root "ucchi" is declared to mean "to glean," and this [term] generally signifies completion. (76)
The root *dram* preceded by *vi-* means "to go"; likewise, there are *dhraj*, *dhrajit*, *dhṛj*, *dhṛji*, *dhvaj*, and *dhvajī*. Furthermore, *kūj* is said to mean "an indistinct sound. (77)
*Arja* and *arja* are used in the sense of acquisition; *garja* is used in the sense of sound; *tarjati* is used in the sense of threatening;
*karjati* is used in the sense of distress; and *kharja* is used in the sense of honoring. (78)
The root *aja* is recorded as meaning "to go," "to impel," and "to protect"; it is also associated with splendor (*tejas*).
*Khaja* refers to churning; *khaji*, however, denotes a defect in movement, while *ejṛ* signifies trembling or motion. (79)
The root *kam* is said to mean "to tremble" (*kampane*), while *sphūrj* and *vajranirghoṣa* are derived from *oṭu*.
The root *kṣi* is proclaimed as being used intransitively (*akarmaka*) in the sense of "destruction" (*kṣaye*), and this is cited as ending in a vowel (*ajanta*). ||80||
However, because its causal meaning is internalized, it is cited as transitive;
this root *kṣīj* (to emit sound) is capable of being read with *kūj* in the list of roots beginning with *avyakta-śabda*. ||81||
The roots *laj* and *lāj* are used in the sense of parching; *lāj* and *lāji* in the sense of reproaching;
*jaj*, *jajī*, and *jajī* in the sense of battle; and *tuj* is said to mean injury. (82)
The root *tuji* is used in the sense of protecting; *gaja*, *gaji*, and *gṛji* are used in the sense of sound;
*muja* and *muji* are also used here in the sense of sound; and *gaja* is proclaimed to be used in the sense of intoxication.
The roots *vaja* and *vrata* are said to mean "going," and they all have anudātta as their indicatory vowel (*anubandha*).
Then, the last [vowels] of the eight groups, ending with the thirty-sixth consonant (ṣa), are [the *mātrikās*]. ||84||
Among these roots, the first, *aṭṭ*, is used in the sense of eating and transgressing; some declare that this root has *d* as its penultimate letter, while others say it has *t*. (85)

*Veṣṭ* is used in the sense of surrounding; *ceṣṭa* is used in the sense of movement; *goṣṭala* and *loṣaṭ* are used in the sense of a collection; *ghaṭṭ* is used in the sense of moving; and *sphuṭa* is indeed used in the sense of blossoming. (86)
Then both Vaṭhi and Maṭhikaṭhī entered upon the practice of solitary wandering;
for *śoka* is said to mean sorrowful reflection, while *muṭhi* means protection. (87)
The root *heṭh* is used in the sense of affliction; *eṭhati* is [also] used there, as is *hiḍ*.
*Huḍ* is said to mean movement and non-agitation, while *huḍi* refers to the act of gathering. 88.
The roots *kuḍi*, *dāha*, and *vaṇḍati* signify burning; *maṇḍati* signifies dividing;
*bhaṇḍati* is said to mean reviling; and *bhaḍi* signifies reviling as well. (89)
It is said that *nindā* and *upālambhana* refer to censure, while *parihāsa* refers to jesting. The word *piḍi* is declared to mean a collection, and *muḍi* is used in the sense of cleansing. (90)
Nyagbhāva (subordination) and śuddhi (purity) are proclaimed as mārjana (cleansing).
The root tuḍi is said to mean "striking" (stuḍane), and its derivative, stoḍana, is explained here in this context. 91.
*Dāraṇa* means splitting and *hiṃsana* means harming; furthermore, *huḍi* is used in the sense of obstructing (*varaṇa*).
*Varaṇa* is said to mean acceptance, while others have declared it to mean seizing (*haraṇa*). ||92||
The root *caḍi* is remembered in the senses of anger, disease, and a collection;
*taḍi* is said to mean striking; and *paḍi* is cited in the sense of going. (93)
The root *kaḍi* is used in the sense of intoxication, *khaḍi* in the sense of churning, and *huḍṛ* and *hoḍṛ* in the sense of disrespect;
*dāḍṛ* and *mat* are used in the sense of swimming, and the group beginning with *saba* is also accepted [in this sense]. (94)
The root *āplu* is said to mean "to float," while *drāḍṛ* is likewise used in the sense of "falling apart.
Then there is *dhrāḍṛ*, and subsequently *ślāghāyām* (in the sense of praising) follows *śāḍṛ*. 95.
The root *pū* (to fill) ending in the group of eight [roots] takes the *parasmaipada* endings;
*ṣaḍaśīti* is proclaimed as meaning "boasting," while *śauṭṭa* means "pride" and *yauṭṛ* means "binding. (96)
In the case of *unmāda*, [the root] *mṛ* with the prefix *ud-* ending in *ḍā* is the second [type];
this is recited among those ending in *nāthi* and *vaṭ* due to the similarity of meaning. 97.
The roots *varṣ* and *vṛṇ* mean "to rain"; *kaṭ* and some say *caṭ* mean "to weave";
*da*, *avaṭ*, and *paṭ* mean "to give"; and *raṭ* means "to speak. (98)
The root *śaṭ* is accepted by the wise in the sense of childhood, destruction, disease, movement, and exhaustion; *vaṭ* is said to mean enveloping. (99)
The two roots *kiṭ* and *khaṭ* are said to mean "fear"; however, those same two, when preceded by *śi*, mean "to spit.
*Jaṭ* and *jhaṭ* signify "disrespect," while *bhaṭati* signifies "assembling" and "supporting. (100)
The root *taṭ* is said to mean height; *khaṭ* is remembered in the sense of desire.
*Ṇaṭ* is used for dancing, *piṭ* for sound and a collection, while *haṭ* is that same [sound]. (101)
The root *dīp* is used in the sense of "shining," while *luṭ* is used in the sense of "stirring.
Some say this [root *luṭ*] ends in *ḍ*; *ciṭ* is recorded in the sense of "forest" and "service for others. (102)
The word *viṭ* is said to mean "sound," while in the sense of "reviling" it belongs to the *baśādi* group; some say *hiṭ*, and there is also *iṭ*. Furthermore, *kiṭ* and *kaṭī* mean "to go. (103)
Some call that [root] the third, while others call it *ī*; other wise men, however, say that by joining the two roots together, another [root] is formed. (104)
The root *maḍ* is said to mean "adornment," *kuṭ* means "deficiency" as its action;
*puḍ* and *pruḍ* signify "crushing," *gṛd* signifies "becoming small," and *cuḍ* is recorded [to mean] "remembrance. (105)
Some declare *muḍi* in the sense of breaking (*khaṇḍana*), while others say *puḍi* means "and so forth" (*cetyapara*).
Some state *ruṭi* and *luṭi* mean theft (*steya*), while others say *ruṭhi* and *luṭhī*. 106.
Others say that *ruḍ* and *luṭ* [are used] in this sense; *sphuṭi* is recorded in the sense of "bursting open.
Thus some declare it, reading it as *paṭ* in the section on unmanifest speech (*avyaktavāci*). 107.
The word *vaṭha* is used by the learned in the sense of stoutness; *maṭha* is said to mean both a dwelling and intoxication; and *kaṭha* is declared to mean a difficult livelihood and reproach. (108)
*Raṭaḥ* is said [to mean] "noise," while some say *raṭha*; *haṭhaḥ* means "leaping" and "deceit. Some say it means "force"; furthermore, there are *ruṭha*, *luṭha*, and *uṭha*. (109)
The three [prefixes] *upa*, *ut*, and *ni* are said by some to have the sense of "affliction";
*saṃ* is used in the sense of "defilement" and "injury," as well as in the sense of "deceit. (110)

In this context, *śuṭha* would mean "deceitful" (*śaṭha*) regarding obstruction; however, the Master has stated that it is *śuṭhī*, and likewise, *kuṭhi* occurs here in the same sense of the action. (111)
The root *luṭh* is used in the sense of striking and laziness; *śuṭhi* is used in the sense of drying;
*ruṭhi* and *luṭhi* are used in the sense of motion; and *cuḍḍ* is said to be used in the sense of making something one's own. (112)
They say that the cause of its manifestation is the indication of one's intention (*abhiprāya*).
*Aḍḍa*, *abhiyoga*, and *kakārkaśya*—these three, along with *kaḍḍa* and *cuḍḍā*, [are the causes]. (113)
Furthermore, there are the verbal roots *krīḍṛ* in the sense of playing, *tuḍṛ* and *toḍane* (to strike) [as well as] *tūḍṛ*;
some, however, say that *huḍṛ* and *huḍṛ* are used in the sense of going. (114)
Hoḍṛ and rauḍṛ are also [roots], while loḍṛ is for the action of disrespect;
roḍṛ and loḍṛ are used in the sense of madness, whereas hyaḍ is recorded for the act of exertion. ||115||

The root *laḍ* is said to mean "play" (*vilāsa*); furthermore, due to the identity between *ḍa* and *la*, and *la* and *la*, masters such as Svāmī and others have declared that the verbal root is *lal*. 116.
Others say that *kaḍa* means intoxication, while here it denotes movement;
its location is said to be a part of the mouth, and its final letter belongs to the *pa*-group (the labials). 17.
The thirty-four roots ending with *stobh* have the low-pitched (*anudātta*) accent as their indicatory mark (*anubandha*).
Among these, the first root, *tipṛ*, meaning "to sprinkle" (*pṛkṣa*), occurs in the sense of sprinkling. (118)
Kṣīrasvāmī recorded [the root] as being anudātta, yet he erred by thinking it was seṭ;
tepṛ is used in the sense of trembling, and galepṛ is said to mean "to shake. (119)

The root *ṭu-vepṛ* is declared to mean "trembling"; *kepṛ*, *glepṛ*, and *gepṛ*—according to the division of the sūtras, Svāmī [Durgasiṃha] states that these also mean trembling, and [the last] also movement. (120)

But Maitreya, having recited [the verse], says that [the word] "here" (iha) is expected [to mean] "in this [world]" (asmin loke), because of the difference in meaning; thus says the son of Glepa. (121)
Furthermore, it is recited: "mepṛ, repṛ, and lepṛ are recorded as meaning 'to go';
trapūṣ and syā are used here for 'shame'; and kapi is said to mean 'movement'. (22)
*rab* and *labi* are recorded as being used in the sense of sound;
*kabṛ* is indeed used for color and lack of modesty; and *klībṛ* and *kṣībṛ* are recorded in the sense of intoxication. ||123||
The root *rebhṛ* occurs in the sense of making sound; *śībhṛ* and *cībhṛ* occur in the same meaning.
In some places, *rabhi* is also recited, as well as *ṣṭabhi* and *skabhi*. (124)
Some say that *stambha* is intended for obstruction; it is used in the sense of natural paralysis.
*Jṛbh* occurs in the bending of limbs, while *śalb* is used in the sense of speaking falsely. (125)

The root *valbh* is used in the sense of eating, beginning with the dental and labial sounds; *galbh* is used in the sense of audacity; and *śrambh*, which is accepted as beginning with both dentals and palatals, is used in the sense of negligence. (126)
Indeed, these forty-one roots beginning with *gup* and ending with *sibh* are parasmaipada roots, occurring here in the *ṣṭubh* meter and the *stamba* section. (127)
The root *gup* preceded by *pra* is used in the sense of protection; *dhūp* is used in the sense of heating; *jap* and *jalp* [are used] for speech.
It is proclaimed that *jap* refers to distinct speech, while it is also prescribed for mental [recitation]. 128.
The letter *da* is said to be used for conciliation (*sāntvana*), while *ṣa* is traditionally taught for conjunction (*samavāya*).
Conjunction, moreover, is either a connection or indeed a correct understanding. 129.
The roots *rapati* and *lapati* are proclaimed to mean "distinct speech";
however, *cupati* is said to mean "slow movement" and also "injury. (130)
Tupa, tumpau, trupa, trumpau, trupha, tumbhau, trupha, and stataḥ; and among these, the first two, the fifth, and the sixth are [the long ones]. 131.
The first four [names] are without the letter *r*, while the subsequent four have *r*.
The next eight end in the nominative case (*prathamānta*), and those following end in the accusative case (*dvitīyānta*); these are declared to be with the vowel *ā*. 132.
Parpa, pharpa, arba, parba, larba, and barbati; marba, karba, kharba, garva, śarbha, sarva, and carbati. ||133||
The first [word] here ends in the nominative case; then both end in the accusative case;
then eleven end in the instrumental case, excluding the second one. 134.
And it is remembered that in this Daṇḍaka meter, all [the syllables] have the letter 'ra' (repha) as the third;
'kubi' is prescribed for covering, while 'lubi' and 'tubi' are considered for crushing.
*ṣṛbhu* and *ṣṛmbhu* are used in the sense of "striking," while *ṣibhu* and *ṣimbhu* are others;
furthermore, *śubha* and *śumbha* are used in the sense of "speaking. (136)
Some say that these two [roots] mean "to shine," while others say they mean "to injure.
Now, those ending in a nasal (anunāsika) shall have anudātta as their indicatory mark (anubandha). 137.
The roots *kamvanta*, *daśa*, *ghiṇya*, and others are used in the sense of seizing; *ghiṇi* and *ghuṇi* [are also used there].
Furthermore, *ghṛṇi* and *ghṛṇa* are proclaimed [to mean] heat, while *ghūrṇa* is proclaimed in the sense of whirling. (138)
These two [roots] are *parasmaipada*; however, they will appear in the *tudadi* class.
Furthermore, *paṇ* is used in the sense of bargaining as well as praising, while *pana* is used only in the sense of praising. (139)

*Bhāma* is used in the sense of anger; *kṣamūṣ*, however, occurs in the sense of endurance. Then there is *kamū*, which signifies desire; here *kānti* would mean longing. These [roots] are then conjugated in the *parasmaipada*. (140)
Thirty [roots] ending in *kram* are now enumerated: *hyaṇ*, *raṇa*, *vaṇau*, *bhaṇaḥ*, *maṇaḥ*, *kaṇaśca*, *kvaṇati*, *vraṇati*, *bhraṇati*, and *dhvaṇāḥ*. (141)
In this context, some scholars also read "dhana" as a word for sound; furthermore, the roots *oṇ* and *śoṇ* are used here in the sense of bringing, while *varṇa* and *gati* are also included. 142.
The roots *saṅghṛ*, *śoṇṛ*, and *śloṇṛ* are said to be these three; they begin with the palatal sibilant (*ūṣman*) and are *śoṇṛ*-type roots. Likewise, *paiṇṛ* is used in the sense of "going. (143)
It is used in the senses of impelling and joining; in some places it is read as *praṇiti*.
Indeed, this root *dhaṇ*, ending in *n*, is recorded by the learned in the grammatical tradition as having the sense of sound. (144)
Some [grammarians] also state that *baṇ* means "small," while *kanī* refers to "splendor," "beauty," and "motion.
Furthermore, *ṣṭan* and *vana* are used in the sense of "sound," whereas *vana* and *ṣaṇ* denote "gathering" or "enjoyment. (145)

The roots *amo*, *dramo*, and *hamma* are used in the sense of "going" (*gati*); *mīmṛ* is also used in the sense of "sound" (*śabda*). Furthermore, there are *muścha*, *murja*, *mujha*, and likewise *mū*. (146)
Some read "jimim" in the section on eating; then there would be the "krama" [repetition].
In the case of stepping with the feet, there are those beginning with "ayati" and ending with "revatī. (147)
Indeed, thirty-seven [suffixes] are declared to have anudātta indicatory letters:
gati, ava, āva, vaya, paya, maya, ya, taya, and ūṇaya. (148)
The root *day* is used in the senses of giving, going, and protecting;
*ādāna* is said to mean taking, while *raya* is stated to mean going. (149)

The root *ūyī* is used in the sense of weaving; *pūyī* is used in the sense of perishing, spreading, and foul odor; and *krūyī* is traditionally recorded in the sense of sound and obstructing. ||150||
The root *kṣmāyī* is said to mean "to shake" when used with the prefix *vi-*, while *sphāyī* and *opyāyī* signify "increase.
The root *tāyṛ* means "continuity" or "protection," and that continuity is described as a "string" (*prabandha*). 151.
Śala is proclaimed to mean both "covering" and "moving";
likewise, bala and valla may signify both "covering" and "wandering. (152)
The root *mal* is used in the sense of holding; *bhal* and *bhall*, however, are for the purpose of harming;
and they are proclaimed to denote the action of taking up and conversing. 153.
The root *kala* is used in the sense of sound and counting; *kallati* is used for indistinct sound.
He says that *svāmītva* means "the state of being a master," and *tūṣṇībhāva* means "silence. (154)
In the sense of gambling, there are the roots *tevṛ*, *devṛ*, *savane* (in the sense of pressing), *sevṛ*, and *gevṛ*;
also *glevṛ*, *pevṛ*, *mlevṛ*, and *mevṛ*. Here, another [root] is *sīt* and this one is *yayam*. 155.
The authors of the Nyāsa and other works state that even this [term] is used with an underlying intention (sopadeśa);
however, we consider this statement to be contrary to the Bhāṣya. ||156||
Some excellent scholars also cite *śevṛ* and *vṛkṣevṛ*;
however, *revṛ* occurs in the sense of leaping, and that is considered to be a swift motion. 157.
There are ninety-nine roots ending in *av* that take the *parasmaipada* endings; among them, there are six more.
Of these, three—*mavyati*, *sūrkṣya*, *īrkṣya*, and *īrṣya*—are used in the sense of binding. (158)
The horses are for the purpose of envy in their movement; the pressings are proclaimed as pure. Bathing is indeed the loosening of the limbs of the Soma plants. ||159||
The mixing of grains or the pressing of fermented liquor is proclaimed as *surā*;
some call it *cucya*, while *harya* is recorded in the senses of desire and movement. (160)
The root *ala* is said to mean adorning, warding off, and sufficiency;
some say it means compassion when accented with a svarita; and *phaṇa* with the prefix *sañ* means bursting open. (161)
*Mīla*, *śmīla*, *asmīla*, and *kṣmīla* are used in the sense of closing the eyes;
*nimeṣaṇa*, meaning contraction, begins with the palatal *t* and is the second [term in this group]. (162)
The third [type] begins with *dantya* (dentals) and so forth; then there is *pratiṣṭambha*, which means obstruction, and *pīlati*.
*Pratiṣṭambha* is obstruction, and the color *nīla* is proclaimed [as the fourth]. ||163||
*Śīla* is to be understood as concentration; it is said to be a wedge and a bond.
*Śīla* is remembered as a bank, an obstruction, a disease, and a sound. (164)
It may be cotton; that is known as *niṣkoṣaṇa*.
It is also considered the extraction of what is internal so that it no longer remains outside. ||165||
In the sense of "massing," it is called *pūla*; in the sense of "foundation," it is *mūlati*.
In the sense of "accomplishment," it is *phalati*, and in the sense of "bringing about existence," *culla* is desired. (166)
The manifestation of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is considered by the wise to be the process of *bhāvanā*.
The root *cill* signifies blossoming, expansion, relaxation, and also the act of bringing something into being (*bhāvakṛti*). (167)
Some wise men say that *atil* means "to go," while others say it means "to press oil"; furthermore, there are the roots *vel*, *cel*, *lṛt*, *kel*, *khel*, *kṣvel*, and *vell*. (168)
In the sense of "moving," there are five roots ending in ṛ, with the sixth being said to end in lopa;
namely, velṛ, phelṛ, tathā śelṛ, and pelṛ in the sense of "going"—so say some. (169)
The root *skhal* is said to mean "to stumble," while *khala* is declared to mean "a collection.
*Gal* is used in the sense of "eating," *ṣal* in the sense of "going," and *dal* is recorded as meaning "to split apart. (170)
*Śvala* and *śvallā* are used for swift movement; *kolṛka* and *orṛ* likewise for movement; *dhorṛ* is proclaimed for obstruction, and *gati* for skill in movement. (171)
The root *tsar* is said to mean "deceit" or "guile," and it is also spoken of as meaning "creeping.
The roots *abhra*, *vabhra*, and *abhracara* relate to movement; the root *car* is used for that very purpose of going. (172)
Even in the case of eating, the sound *ṣṭhiv* occurs here with the sense of the action of spitting;
the author of the Vṛtti says that for this second [root], there is either *ṣṭhā* or *ṣṭhi*. (173)
This root *ji* (to conquer) is read as being used with the suffix *aC* (forming *jaya*) among roots ending in vowels;
its attainment of excellence is declared here as its meaning, and it is stated to be intransitive (*akarmaka*). 174.
The word *jīva* is used for the maintenance of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), while both *pīvamī* and *vā* denote fatness;
*tīvanī* and *vā* are recorded as meaning stoutness, and *kṣīvu* and *kṣevū* refer to the human seat.

The root *urvī* is used in the sense of spreading; likewise, *thurvī*, *durvī*, and *dhurvī* are used in the sense of injury; *gurvī* is declared to mean lifting up; and *murvī* is said to mean binding. (176)
*Pūraṇa*, *parvan*, and *marvan* are recorded as meaning "filling";
*carva* is used for eating; while *bharva* signifies injury, and *karva*, *kharva*, and *garvati* signify pride or arrogance. (177)
The roots *darpa*, *iṣ*, *arva*, and *sarva* are proclaimed to mean "to injure"; *hviṣ* means "to pervade"; and *pivi*, *mivi*, and *ṇivi* are recorded as meaning "to sprinkle. (178)
Some say that the word *mūrdhan* is used with the sibilants (*ūṣman*) and so forth; here they cite the third [meaning].
Another meaning, "service" (*sevana*), is illustrated in the *Taraṅgiṇī*. ||179||
The roots *hivi*, *divi*, *dhivi*, and *jivi* are proclaimed to have the meaning of "to please"; *ravi*, *aravi*, and *dhavi* are said to have the meaning of "to go. (180)
The root *kṛ* is traditionally taught as meaning "to injure" and "to do," while *gā* is recorded in the sense of "motion.
It is recited in the *svādi* group [of roots], and this very root *mav* is intended to mean "binding. (181)
It must necessarily [be used] in the senses of protecting, going, luster, affection, satisfying, as well as understanding, entering, and even hearing. (182)
It is used in the sense of requesting one's own interest, as well as in the desire for action;
likewise in brilliance, attainment, embracing, and even in injury. (183)
It is proclaimed that [the root] *dhā* is used in the senses of taking up, dividing, and increasing;
however, it is intended as *svarita*-accented in the senses of moving and purifying. 184.
Thereafter, fifty-one roots ending in *īṣ* are *ātmanepadī*; among them, *dhukṣ* is used in the sense of inflaming or kindling, and *dhikṣ* in the sense of afflicting or tormenting. (185)
The root *vṛ* is used in the sense of choosing (*varaṇa*) and in the act of undertaking knowledge (*vidyopādāna*).

*Bhikṣ* is used in the sense of obtaining (*lābha*), not obtaining (*alābha*), and begging (*bhikṣā*). *Kliś* is used in the sense of suffering (*kleśati*). *Sū* is used in the sense of flowing (*sravati*). (186)

He says that when speech is indistinct, there is difficulty; likewise, the root *bādh* is used in the sense of obstructing, while *dakṣ* is used for growth, speed, and skill, as well as for shaving and sacrifice. (187)
The term *īkṣa* is proclaimed in the context of the observances of the initiation (*upanayana*) and the instruction in vows; furthermore, *bhāṣa* is said to refer to distinct speech. (188)
In the sense of "seeing," it is *bhāṣa*; when the voice is manifest, it is called *kathya*.
It is *varṣa* in the sense of "moistening," while in the sense of "sounds" (*geṣu*), it begins with the dentals and labials. || 189 ||
Regarding the desire to obtain, there is *sātrabhaved*; others say that here it is *anveṣaṇam*. They say *gleṣr* is used for effort, while *peṣr*, *jeṣr*, and *ṇeṣr* are also [employed]. 190.

The roots *eṣṛ*, *reṣṛ*, *gatyārtha* (meaning "to go"), *reṣṛ*, *heṣṛ*, and *heṣṛ* [are used here]. Among these, the first refers to an indistinct sound, while *vṛka* is proclaimed to refer to the sound of a wolf. ||191||
In the word *dvādaśva*, the root *kāsṛ* is cited in the sense of censuring sound;
*bhāsṛ* in the sense of shining; *ṇāsṛ* and *rāsṛ* in the sense of sound; and then *kulitvavāk*. 192.
The root *ṇas* (nas) occurs with the prefix *abhi* in the sense of fear; with the prefix *śas*, it is joined with *rāṅ*.
*Gras* and *glasu* are used in the sense of devouring, while *īh* is desired in the sense of exertion. (193)
*Bahiḥ* and *mahiḥ* are used for "external" or "outside"; *vṛddhiḥ* means "increase. *Gataḥ* and *pahiḥ* are said to mean "gone away.
*Garhaḥ* and *galhaḥ* signify "censure," while *barha* and *balhatī* denote "preeminence. (194)

These two roots, *oṣṭhayati* and *māvi*, as well as *varha* and *valha*, are prescribed for the sense of reviling; these two, beginning with *dantya-oṣṭhya*, are proclaimed for the senses of injury and covering. (195)
Some, however, state that the two preceding [roots] begin with a dental and labial, while these two [begin] with a labial;
furthermore, they cite *lpih* and *gatau* as examples.

In the case of *prayatna*, *vehat*, *hehṛ*, *heṣya*, and *abdāhṛ*, the first [consonant] is considered to begin with a dental-labial (*dantoṣṭhya*), while the last is held to be a pure labial (*kevalauṣṭhya*). ||197||
Some say that both [the roots *jehati* and *kṣayati*] begin with a labial; others say they begin with a dental-labial.
*Jehati* is said to mean "going," while *kṣayati* is declared to mean "sleeping" and "wasting away. (198)
Some say that *nikṣepa* means "deposit"; the root *kāśṛ* is proclaimed to mean "to shine.
*Ūha* refers to "reflection," while *gāhū* is declared to mean "stirring" or "agitating. (199)

The root *gṛh* is declared by the wise to mean "seizing," while *glaha* means "gambling. Furthermore, the root *ghuṣ* is said to mean "making beautiful"; some even say it is *ghaṣ* in this sense. (200)
Those ending in the vowel 'a' preceded by the letter 'u' are called *arhatī*;
the remaining ninety roots, which take the *parasmaipada* endings, follow in order. (201)
The root *ghuṣ* is explained as "non-proclamation," whereas that which is "proclamation" is [the meaning of] *vi-ghuṣ*.
Others have said that in a different sense, it means "promising. (202)
Others read *paṭh* as "sound"; *kṣu* and *stan* are taught in the sense of thinning;
*takṣ*, *tvakṣ*, and *ukṣ* are declared in the sense of sprinkling, while *tūkṣ* is desired in that same sense. (203)
The root *rakṣ* is proclaimed to mean "protection," while *ṇikṣ* is said to mean "to kiss.
Furthermore, *tṛkṣ*, *ṭṛkṣ*, and *ṇakṣ* are declared to have the meaning of "motion. (204)
Some say that from the chest and the hips arises what is called the *saṅghāta*;
regarding the *saṅghāta*, some have declared it to be *mrakṣa*, while others have called it *mrakṣa*. (205)
The cutting [of the skin] would be its removal; that would be the extraction of the skin.
Here, "grahaṇa" (seizing) would be one view, while others hold it to be "parigraha" (appropriation). 206.
In some places it is said that *sūrkṣa* means "care" (*ādara*) and *sūrkṣa* means "disregard" (*anādara*); however, that is a corrupt reading (*apapāṭha*).
Therefore, [the correct terms for] contempt and disdain are *avajñā* and *avahelana*, while *asūrkṣaṇa* is the act of not regarding. (207)
Thus it was said by Amara: "The words *kāṅkṣin*, *vākṣin*, and *cakṣimān* denote one who desires; *athadrākṣi*, *dhākṣi*, and *dhvākṣi* are used in the sense of something terrible. (208)
Furthermore, *vāśiti* means "to cry out," while *cūṣa* means "to suck"; *tūṣati* denotes satisfaction;
*vūṣa* occurs in the sense of growth; *mūṣa* means "theft"; and *lūṣati* and *rūṣati* [are used]. (209)
The root *śūṣ* is used in the sense of ornamenting, procreation, and strength; for this [root] is indeed *parṣu*.
The root *yūṣ*, beginning with a palatal and a sibilant (*tālavyoṣmādi*), is recorded in the sense of injury, as is *jūṣ*. (210)

The root *alaṅkṛ* is used in the sense of adorning; *bhūṣ* and *ūṣ* in the sense of pain; *īṣ* in the sense of gathering by gleaning; *kaṣ*, *khaṣ*, *śiṣ*, *jaṣ*, *jhaṣ*, *śaṣ*, *vaṣ*, and *maṣ* [are used in their respective senses]. ||211||

The roots *ruṣ* and *riṣ* have the meaning of "to injure"; the sixth [root] is for praise, while the seventh has the palatal sibilant (*ṣ*) as its initial and the dental-labial sibilant (*s*) as its initial. 212.
In this context, *śiṣ* occurs with an anudātta accent; *bhaṣ* is said to mean "reproaching.
*Bhartsanam* is declared to be the barking of dogs, while *uṣ* is proclaimed to mean "burning. (213)
The roots jiṣu, viṣu, and miṣu are declared to mean "to sprinkle.
Here, viṣu is anudātta (unaccented); phuṣa is the sixth; and there are śriṣu and śliṣu. 214.
The roots *pruṣ* and *pluṣ* are used in the sense of burning; this [root] *śliṣ* is known as being with the augment *iṭ*.
They state that the inclusion of the root belonging to the *divādi* class [is for the sake of inclusion] among those that do not take the augment *iṭ*. (215)
Kaiyaṭa and others maintain that the author of the Nyāsa intended the mention of both [types of roots];
however, that which was stated regarding "those not taking the augment iṭ" contradicts his own statement. (216)
We consider that [the reading] should also be disregarded because it contradicts other lexicons;
for *pṛṣu*, *vṛṣu*, and *mṛṣu* are proclaimed to mean "to sprinkle. (217)
The root *mṛṣ* is considered to mean "to endure" and "to harm," while two others are held to mean "affliction.
*Ghṛṣ* is said to mean "friction," and *hṛṣ* is declared to mean "falsehood. (218)
The roots *tuṣ* (to satisfy), *hras* (to shorten), *hlās* (to fade), and *rās* (to sound) are fully proclaimed [in this context].
*Las* is used in the sense of clinging (*śleṣaṇa*), while *ghaslṛ* is used in the sense of playing (*krīḍana*) and eating (*adana*). ||219||
The roots *jarja*, *carya*, and *jharjh* are declared to mean "to revile" and "to injure," as well as "to threaten. The roots *pisṛ* and *pesṛ* are traditionally held to mean "to go. (220)
The root *has* is said to mean "to laugh," while *ṇiś* is declared to mean "meditative absorption" (*samādhi*).
This [root] would be the last of the palatal sibilants (*tālavyoṣman*), and likewise there are *miś* and *maś*. (221)
In the word *roṣakṛte*, there is the sound *caṭa*; these two [consonants] are palatal sibilants (*tālavyoṣman*).
The sound *śava* ends with a dental-labial [sibilant]; the palatal sibilant *aṭ* indicates motion. 222.
This [letter] 'śa', which is palatal, a sibilant, and the last of its class, is considered to have a protracted (pluta) movement in the sense of "going.
It is designated as 'śasu' in the sense of "injury" and is recognized as being dental and ending in a sibilant. ||223||
Śaṃsu is used in the sense of praise; this [root] is also used in the sense of difficulty or distress.
Parikalkana is declared to be deceit, for kalkana is indeed guile. 224.
The root *bṛṃhati* is said to mean sound; *raha* is used in the sense of abandonment, and *rahi* in the sense of motion.
*Dṛha*, *dṛhi*, *bṛha*, and *bṛhi* are proclaimed to signify growth. (225)

The root *bṛṃhati* is said to mean "sound," while some have declared that *bṛhi* has the same meaning. The roots *tuhi*, *duhi*, and *ruhi* are said to mean "injury," whereas *arha* means "worship. (226)
The twenty-five verbal roots ending in *kṛp* are those with an anudātta (low-pitched) accent.
*Dyuta* is recorded as meaning "to shine," *śvitā* as "color," and *ñimidā* as "moistening. (227)
The root *niṣvad* is proclaimed to mean both "to moisten" and "to release";
some have stated that the word "release" (*mocana*) in this context means "to delude. (228)
Some say that *ñikṣvidā* means "to sound," while *ruc* is traditionally taught in the sense of "shining";
furthermore, *ghoṭati* occurs in the sense of "turning around" or "wandering. (229)
*ruṭ*, *luṭ*, and *uṭha* are proclaimed to denote resistance; *śubha* denotes radiance; *kṣubha* denotes agitation; *na bhatu* and *bhautu* [denote] those two. 230.
These two [roots] were stated today as being used in the sense of violence (hiṃsā), even though they do not exist [as such];
for they are seen in the *divādi* group and the *krayādi* group due to a difference in form. ||231||
The roots *sraṃsu*, *dhvaṃsu*, and *bhraṃsu* are declared to mean "to fall down" (*avasaṃsan*).
Some authorities have also recited *dhvaṃsu* in the sense of "motion" (*gati*) and *bhraṃśu* as well. 232.
Others declare that in this context, the third [root] alone ends in the palatal *t* (i.e., *bhraṃśati*).
In the *divādi* class, there are both *bhraṃśu* and *bhaṃśu*, signifying falling downwards. ||233||
In the sense of "trust," it becomes *śrambhuḥ*; this word is said to begin with a dental [sibilant].
When beginning with a palatal [sibilant], as mentioned previously, it was stated to mean "negligence. (234)

The root *vṛt* is used in the sense of turning and increasing; *vṛdh* in the sense of the sound of contempt; *śṛdh* in the sense of trickling; *syand* is used in the sense of flowing; and *kṛp* is traditionally taught in the sense of capability. (235)
The root *vṛt* is used to indicate the completion of both the *dyutādi* and *vṛtādi* groups;
furthermore, the roots ending in *svarati* shall have anudātta indicatory marks (*anudāttānubandhaka*). 236.
There are thirteen [types of characters]; among them, at the outset, in the context of action, the *ghaṭa* (pot) is mentioned.
The *vyādha* (hunter) occurs in fear, agitation, and in the performance of famous deeds. (237)
The root *kath* is said to mean "to spread," and *pra-sa* is called "extension.
*Mrad* is declared to mean "crushing," and *skand* is used in the sense of the action of "leaping" or "moving forward. (238)
*Vidrāvaṇa* means putting to flight; *kadana* means slaughter. *Kṣaj* is used in the senses of going and giving.
*Dakṣa* is used in the senses of going and injuring; this same root [in the past tense] was previously used in the senses of going and swiftness. (239)
The root *krap*, which is listed among the anudātta roots, is cited again here for the sake of its inclusion in the *mit* class;
it signifies compassion (*kṛpā*) as well as going. Similarly, there are *kandati*, *krandati*, and *kladi*. (240)
Some say that "vaikalya" denotes dejection;
however, the Lord Nandi has stated that all three [terms] signify dejection. (241)
Maitreya considers that there may be the roots *krad*, *kradī*, *atredī*, *anidit* *krad*, and also *klad*; he recognizes this distinction here. (242)
Furthermore, among the roots conjugated in the *parasmaipada*, *kad*, *krad*, and *kland* are said here to denote calling out and weeping, respectively. ||243||

This reading [of *mit*] is for the sake of the ātmanepada; however, here *ñī* signifies haste (*tvarā*). In this context, *sambhrama* means agitation. Here, the roots beginning with *ghaṭ* are declared to have the *ṣit* designation. (244)
Now, those ending in *phaṇ* are declared in order to be *parasmaipada*:
*jvar* in the sense of disease, *gaḍ* in the sense of sprinkling, and *heḍ* in the sense of surrounding. (245)

Among those roots marked with the anudātta accent that signify "going," the root *hī* (in the sense of "disregard") alone—when its indicatory letter (*anubandha*) has been removed—is used here according to the distinction of meaning. (246)
Here, the *jvarādi* group is cited separately from the general list for the purpose of establishing its status as having a *mit* marker;
apart from this specific mention, it belongs to the class of *anuvāda* (reiterations) occurring in the middle section.
For by implication, the *parasmaipada* ending occurs here;
thus, both "vaṭu" and "bhaṭa" would also be [used] in the sense of the act of reviling. (248)

The two roots *vaṭ* and *vaṣṭ*, which were previously mentioned as being included in the *bhṛt* group, are stated here for the sake of the designation *mit*; for they apply specifically to the act of speaking. (249)
The actor who was previously mentioned is here restated as performing the dance; in this regard, the following distinction should be understood: those [who perform] are the actors. (250)
But designation (vyapadeśa) consists of drama, which is characterized by the representation of the meaning of a sentence;
it is that which occurs again among those who perform the meaning of what was previously recited. (251)
That which consists of the representation of the meaning of words through the gestures of a dancer is called *nṛtya* (dramatic dance);
whereas that which consists of the movement of limbs according to musical rules is *nṛtta* (pure dance). ||252||

Furthermore, that which is stated to be the meaning of the root *naṭ* in the context of a jar and so forth—some indeed read it as "the jar and so forth are *naṭaḥ*, [meaning] they have perished (*natāḥ*). (253)
Others say that because the author of the Bhāṣya taught it again with the suffix *natāv* (in the sense of the agent),
and because he read *nāṭī* with a long vowel, this [suffix] *naṭati* occurs in words such as *ghaṭa*.
All the learned authorities state that *syaṇṇa* is indeed an instruction [for the following].
However, *ṣṭaka* is used in the sense of striking, while *caka* is proclaimed to mean satisfaction. (255)

For that [root] which was previously recited as being used in the sense of both satiation and obstruction, it is here restated in this list solely for the purpose of its having the *mit* designation. 256.
Since it is recited here again among the *ātmanepada* verbs, it is indeed the *parasmaipada* [form] due to the force of this restatement. ||257||
*Kakhe* is said to mean "to laugh"; *śaṅkāyām* (in doubt) is expressed [by *kaṅke*]; *rage* (in passion) is expressed [by *kaṅge*].
*Lage* means "attachment," as do *hrage* and *hlage*; likewise, *ṣage* and *ṣṭhage*. (258)
There may be four [consonants] in the case of *saṃvaraṇa* due to their specific distinction; therefore, *ka* and *ga* are not mentioned.
Both *aka* and *aga* would occur at the end in the case of the curved (*kuṭilā*) movement. 259.
The roots *kaṇ*, *raṇ*, and *caṇ* are said to mean "to go" or "to give," while others state that *śaṇ* and *śraṇ* also mean "to go. (260)
Furthermore, *kratha*, *krathā*, and *klatha* are recorded as having the sense of injury;
likewise, *canaś* and *vanuś* are used, while *jvala* is said to denote blazing. (261)
This [root], which will be recited for the sake of the meaning "to go," is here restated as having the *mittva* designation;
however, *hvala* and *hvalau* are recorded in the sense of "moving," while *smṛ* is proclaimed in the sense of "recollection. (262)
In the context of *cintā* (reflection), there is a summary for the sake of [avoiding] the elision of the vowel in the term *adhyāna* which is to be explained;
here, *adhyāna* is defined as recollection preceded by intense longing (*autkaṇṭhya*). ||263||
In the case of *dṛ*, which belongs to the kryādi class, the rule regarding its being a *mit* vowel is restated here;
however, for *śrā*, which signifies cooking, this is an imitation of the form *śrota*. 264.
One should know that [the root] *jñā* is used for killing, pleasing, and perceiving; Mādhava states that perceiving (*niśāmana*) is visual knowledge. 266.
Others, however, say it is "mere cognition," while another reading is "in sharpenings" (niśāneṣu); that [latter] is said to mean the act of sharpening. ||267||
The root *cal* is used in the sense of trembling; *mi* is used in the sense of strengthening (*ūrjana*).
Here, the root *mī*, belonging to the curādigaṇa, is mentioned in its own form (*svārtha*) without the causal suffix (*ṇic*), for the purpose of [demonstrating] its status as a *mit* root. (268)
The root *ūrj*, meaning "to exert oneself," belongs to the sixth class (*tudādigaṇa*) because it possesses multiple meanings;
it was previously mentioned in the section on *vilāsa* (sportiveness), and its *laṅ* form is used in the sense of "tongue-lashing" (*jihvonmathana*). || 269 ||
The root *mad* with the prefix *un-* signifies making known; likewise, it means dejection.
With the prefix *ni-*, it denotes joy, while dejection is indeed declared to be depression. (270)
The mention of this [root] is stated for the sake of the *mittva* (the designation of *mit*) of the *daivādika* group;
for here, this [root] *dhvan*, meaning "sound," is cited as being subject to *mittva*. 271.
In this [verse], Bhoja read "dalirvali," "sskhaliraṇī," "dhvaniśca," "trapi reva ca," and "kṣapiśca"; among these, "dhvani" refers to the sound "raṇaḥ. (272)

The roots *dalati*, *rvalati*, *skhalati*, and likewise *strapati*—the vowel in the causative (*nic*) of these becomes short; furthermore, in the case of *kṣai* in the sense of destruction (*kṣaye*), it is likewise. ||273||
That which is to be explained hereafter is now indicated, preceded by the augment *pu*;
the root *svan* is mentioned for the sake of its being designated as having the marker *mit* when used in the sense of "adorning" (*avataṃsane*), as will be explained later.
The view is that this is a *gaṇa-sūtra* stating "the words beginning with *ghaṭa* are measured" (*mita*);
another view is that it consists of the words *janī*, *jṛṣ*, *krasu*, *rañj*, and *mantṛ*. (275)
Some read *ṣṇasu* here in place of *knasu*, for [the root] *jval*, *hval*, and *hyal* undergo modification upon contact with prefixes. 276.
The designation *mittva* (the status of being a *mit* vowel) is intended for those [roots] that exist excluding their present-tense forms;
or else, *mittva* applies even to *glai*, *snai*, *van*, and *vam*, provided they are without prefixes (*upasarga*). 277.
The shortening of the vowel *m* [in *kāmyati*] is taught as occurring before the suffix *amic*;
however, the state of being *mit* does not apply here [to the root *yam*] when it means "not serving food. (278)
In this [treatise], however, it is not desired for the [root] following *skhada* and *rava*;
nor does Nyāsakāra accept the designation *mit* even for that which follows *apa*. (279)
The root *phaṇ* occurs in the sense of "going" (gati), while *vṛt* is used here for the purpose of completion (*pūrti*) for roots beginning with *ghaṭ*;
some wise men here state that *vṛt* follows after *phaṇ*. (280)
The root *svarit*ed* rājṛ, meaning "to shine," has an indicatory vowel (anubandha) that is anudātta;
likewise, the three roots bhrājṛ, bhrāśṛ, and bhlāśṛ, all meaning "to shine," are also declared to be reduplicated (dvit). ||281||
The second and third [roots] are proclaimed to end in the palatal [consonant *c*]. Those beginning with *syam* and ending with *kṣarati* are considered to be parasmaipada (active voice). 282.
The roots *syam*, *svan*, and *dhvan* denote sound; likewise, *ṣam* and *ṣṭamati* denote the absence of deficiency.
*Jval* is said to mean blazing, while *cala*, *kampa*, and *nana* are said to mean trembling. (283)
The root *jala* denotes sharpness in the act of striking; it is thus declared by the wise that "striking" (*ghātana*) is its meaning.
However, *ṭalaṭvalau* signify agitation, and *ṣṭala* is proclaimed to occur in place of *sthāna*. (284)

Some say that *hal* is used in the sense of scratching, *gandha* in the sense of binding, and *ṇal* also in the sense of binding; furthermore, they say *pal* is used for going and *bal* for the act of breathing. 285.
In the context of a granary, the word *pula* is used to denote greatness;
and here, in the sense of a gathering among kinsmen, the word *kula* is said to be synonymous with *bandhu*.
Indeed, its function is perceived here as contraction (saṃstyāna) or gathering (saṃhati).
The roots śal, hula, and pallṛ are used in the sense of moving and in the act of cooking. (287)
The root *kvath* is used in the sense of going (*gati*), while *math* is used in the sense of churning (*viloḍana*).
*Vam* (from *ṭu vam*) is used in the sense of vomiting (*udgiraṇa*), and *bhram* is recorded in the sense of wandering or moving about (*calana*). ||288||
Now, the roots beginning with *kas* are declared to be *parasmaipada* in their respective order:
*ṣadl* (meaning "to dissolve," "to go," and also "to sink down") is *aniṭ*. ||290||
This root *śad*, which is intransitive (*aniṭ*) and signifies the act of breaking, is now indicated as having "breaking" (*śātana*) as its object. (291)
The root *kruś* is without the augment *iṭ* in the senses of calling and crying out;
then there is *idhokti* in the sense of mixing, crookedness, obstruction, and scratching. (292)

Furthermore, there would be the arrival at the Buddha, the birth from the seed, the manifestation, and the movement; however, in this context, the formation of the *vṛt* suffix occurs with the root *kas*. (293)
This has been proclaimed for the purpose of indicating the completion of the *jvalādi* group;
now those ending in *gūh* are stated in their proper sequence according to the *svarita* accent. (294)
The sound *hikka* is said to denote the indistinct; *añcu*, however, is used in the sense of motion and begging.
Some say the root is *acu*, others *āhi*, and still others declare it to be *aci*. (295)
The root *yācṛ* is used in the sense of begging (*yāñcā*); *reṭṛ* is used in the sense of reproaching (*paribhāṣaṇa*).
*Cat* and *dad* are used in the sense of begging (*yācana*); furthermore, *prodhṛ* is declared to mean sufficiency (*paryāpti*). (296)
The root *mid* and *medṛ* are proclaimed to mean "intelligence" and "injury" respectively;
Svāmī says that these two end in *th*, whereas Nyāsa says they end in *dh*. (297)
The term *medhṛ* denotes a gathering; *ṇidṛ* and *īdṛ* denote contempt;
*sannikarṣa* denotes proximity; and *śṛdhū* and *mudhū* are said to mean anointing. (298)
The root *unda* is said to mean "moistening," while *budh* is declared to mean "awakening.
*Ubindir* is used in the sense of "settling," and *veṇṛ* is used for both "knowledge" and "reflection. (299)

The word *gati* is used in the senses of going, perceiving, and also taking up musical instruments; there is no end to its instruction. Furthermore, *khanuḥ* is used in the sense of restriction. (300)
The root *cīvṛ* is used in the senses of taking and restraining; *āyṛ*, however, is used in the sense of honoring.
*Niśam* is used in the sense of hearing, and *vyaya* is said to mean going. (301)
Others have sung that *dāśṛ* means "to give" and *bheṣṛ* means "to fear";
*bhreṣṛ* and *bleṣṛ* mean "to go," while *aso* likewise means "to shine" and "to go. (302)
This root *śam*, though ending in a nasal, is used in the sense of touching and affliction;
"touching" (*sparśana*) is said to mean binding, and the root *laṣ* is proclaimed to mean longing. (303)
The root *caṣ* is said to mean eating; *chaṣati* and *jhaṣa* mean injury;
*bhrakṣ* and *bhlakṣ* mean taking and concealing; and [the root *bhakṣ*] means eating. (304)

Maitreya says that *bhakṣ* is used in the sense of eating; *dāśṛ* is proclaimed in the sense of giving; *māhra* in the sense of measuring; and *guhū*, being ṅit, is used respectively in the sense of concealing and hiding. (305)

Five roots ending in vowels are enumerated; *śriñ* is proclaimed in the sense of service (*sevā*), *bhṛñ* in the sense of supporting (*bharaṇa*), *hrīñ* in the sense of taking away (*haraṇa*), and *dhṛñ* is proclaimed in the sense of holding (*dhāraṇa*). ||306||
The four roots beginning with *bhṛ*—namely *ṇī*, *ñī*, *prāpaṇe* (the root *pā*), and *bhṛ*—are declared to be aniṭ.
Now, those ending in vowels that take the parasmaipada endings are described in their proper sequence. (307)
The root *dheṭ* signifies drinking; likewise, *glai* and *mlai* are said to denote the loss of joy (*harṣakṣaya*).
Here, the learned declare that the loss of bodily constituents (*dhātukṣaya*) is expressed by the term "loss of joy. (308)
The root *dyai* is used in the sense of disrespect; disrespect (*nyakkṛti*) is synonymous with contempt (*tiraskriyā*).
*Drai* occurs in the sense of sleep; *dhai*, however, is recorded in the sense of satisfaction; and *dhyai* is known to be used in the sense of reflection. (309)
The roots *śai* and *ṣṭyai* are used for the sense of sound; *khad* is used for eating; then *khai* is used for wandering.
*Kṣai*, *jai*, and *ṣai* are said to mean destruction (*kṣaye*); *kai* and *gai* are declared to mean sound (*śabde*). 310.
The root *śai* is used in the sense of cooking (*pāka*), while *vai* and *ca* are used in the sense of purification (*śocana*).
*Ṣṭai* occurs in the sense of surrounding (*veṣṭana*), whereas *ṇṣai* is declared to be used in the sense of enveloping (*veṣṭana*). ||311||
Some say that this [root] is used in the sense of beauty (*śobhā*), while others hold it to mean shining (*dīpti*) or purifying (*śodhana*).
*Pā* is used in the sense of drinking (*pāna*), and *ghrā* is proclaimed to be used in the sense of perceiving odors (*gandhopādāna*). 312.
The root *dhmā* is proclaimed by the wise to denote both sound and contact with fire;
here, "contact with fire" refers to the joining of the breath from the mouth with fire. (313)
The root *ṣṭhā* means "to stand" or "to remain"; it is said that when preceded by *pra*, it means "to exert oneself.
*Dā* means "giving," *hvṛ* means "crookedness," and *svṛ* means "sound" and "affliction. (314)
The root *smṛ* is recorded in the sense of recollection and restraint; it is traditionally taught as having two meanings when used with the prefix *su*, namely "to go" and "to remember.
The root *ṛ* occurs in the senses of going and causing to attain; likewise, *gṛ* and *ghṛ* are recorded in the sense of sprinkling. (315)
The root *dhvṛ* is recorded in the sense of reeling or falling; *sru* and *ṣṣu* are remembered in the senses of flowing and sovereignty, respectively.
*Prasava*, however, means permission, while *śru* is proclaimed in the sense of hearing. (316)
The root *dur* is used in the sense of firmness (*dhruva-sthairye*), going (*gatau*), and overcoming (*abhibhave*); it is also recorded in the sense of memory (*smṛtau*).
Furthermore, "overcoming" (*abhibhava*) is understood as either the performance of a lesser action (*nyūna-kriyā*) or the state of being diminished (*nyūnī-bhāva*). ||317||
In the first case, it should be known as transitive (sakarmaka), while in the other, it is also intransitive (akarmaka).
These roots beginning with *dhēṭ* and ending in vowels are traditionally held to be *aniṭ* (not taking the augment *iṭ*). ||318||
Now, the roots ending in *ṅ* that take the *ātmanepada* endings are described;
*smiṅ* is used for slight laughter, and *guṅ* is proclaimed for indistinct sound. (319)

The root *gāṅ* is proclaimed to mean "motion," while *kuṅ*, *huṅ*, and *ṅuṅ* are said to mean "sound. Others, however, state that *tahku*, *ṅkhu*, *guṅ*, *ghuṅ*, and *dṛṅ* have these same meanings. (320)
The roots *cyuñ*, *yuṅ*, *pruṅ*, and *pluṅ* are to be known as such; some indeed read them as *kluṅ*.
The root *ruṅ* is said to mean "going" and "anger," for anger is indeed a form of violence. (321)
The root *dhṛṅ* is used in the sense of "not falling away" (*apadhvaṃsana*); furthermore, *meṅ* is traditionally recorded by me in the sense of "bestowing" (*praṇidāna*).
Bestowing is understood as an exchange (*vinimaya*) or even a restitution (*pratyarpaṇa*). ||322||

*Deṅ* is used in the senses of protecting and going; *śyaiṅ* and *pyaiṅ* [are used] for increasing; *traiṅ* is for protecting; *pūṅ* is for purifying; *mūṅ* is for binding—these roots beginning with *sañj* are indeed *aniṭ* (lacking the *iṭ* augment). ||323||
Having abandoned [the previous rules], the root *gā* (to go) takes the suffix *ṅīṅ*; *tṛ* (to cross) is used for leaping and crossing;
and there are eight roots ending in anudātta indicatory letters (*anubandha*) that are conjugated in the *parasmaipada*. (324)
The root *gup* is said to mean "concealment," while *tij* is stated to mean "sharpening.
*Mān* is declared to signify "honoring," and *badh* refers to the act of "binding. (325)
The root *rabh* is declared [in the sense] of impetuosity; *labh* with the suffix *ḍu* is for the action of attaining;
*ṣvañj* is said [to mean] embracing; and *had* [is used] for the voiding of excrement. (326)
These four roots beginning with *rabh* are declared to be *aniṭ* (not taking the augment *iṭ*).
Then, sixteen roots follow in sequence which take the *parasmaipada* (active voice) terminations. 327.
The root *ñī* is used for spitting and the indistinct sound; *skand* is used for drying and going;
*yabh* is declared to mean sexual union; and *ṇamu* is used for bowing and sound. (328)
The roots *gam* and *sṛp* are used in the sense of "going," while *yam* is traditionally held to mean "cessation.
*Tap* is declared to mean "torment," and *tyaj* is proclaimed to mean "abandoning. (330)
The root *sañj* is used in the sense of clinging; *daṃś* in the sense of biting; *dṛśi* in the sense of seeing;
and the drawing out of reality (*tattvākarṣaṇa*) is declared to be the function of *kṛṣ*. (331)
The root *dah* is declared to mean "to reduce to ashes," while *miha* means "to sprinkle.
These fourteen roots, beginning with *skand*, are considered to be *aniṭ* (not taking the augment *i*). ||332||
The root *kī* is declared to mean dwelling and the removal of disease;
this [root] is generally preceded by *vi*. Now, there are eleven verbal roots (dhātus). 333.
The roots beginning with *dā* and ending with *vah* are used according to their respective meanings;
*dā* is prescribed for cutting, while *śā* is declared to mean sharpening. (334)
The root *pac* (ḍupacaṣ) is said to mean "cooking," while *ṣac* is traditionally remembered to mean "conjunction.
*Bhaj* is used in the sense of "service," *rañj* in the sense of "attachment," and *śap* in the sense of "cursing. (335)
The root *tviṣ* is prescribed for brilliance; *yaj* for the worship of gods, for union, and for making;
and *ḍu-vap* is celebrated for the sowing of seeds. (336)
By the term "continuum of the seed," the sowing in the field as well as the taking up of the embryo is fully explained; this same [process] is also intended in the case of cutting. ||337||

The root *vah* is used in the sense of "carrying" and is aniṭ; the roots beginning with *pac* (the first class) are also aniṭ, excluding those ending in *ṣ*. The root *vas* is used in the sense of "dwelling," but this [specific form] takes the *parasmaipada* endings. (338)

The root *veñ* is recorded in the sense of weaving or extending a thread; *vyeñ* is known in the sense of concealing; and *hveñ* is used in the senses of rivalry and sound. All roots beginning with *vas* are devoid of the augment *iṭ*. (339)
The three roots beginning with *veñ* take the *ñi* affix and thus become recipients of both sets of verbal endings (*pada*);
furthermore, two of them take the *parasmaipada* endings, while the remaining two take both. (340)
The root *vṛdh* (vṛdhu) is used in the sense of manifestation or increase; *śvi* (śvi) is used in the sense of growth as well as movement.
The demarcation (*vṛtkṛti*) made here serves as an indication for the completion of the *yajādi* (yaj-ādi) class of roots. ||341||
The *bhvādi* class is an *ākṛtigaṇa*; after *culump* and others, there are still more [roots] included here, and another is traditionally known as being based on Vedic usage (*sautra*). (342)
Others say that this [suffix] occurs in the sense of disgust and compassion as well.
Thus end the roots beginning with *bhū*; now follow the roots beginning with *ad*, which are both parasmaipada; furthermore, there are two [roots] beginning with *tvad* in the sense of eating.
Both of these roots, *hiṃs* and *gati*, are traditionally recorded as being *rhan* (having *ha* as their penultimate letter) and lacking the augment *iṭ*. ||1||
Four roots beginning with *svarati* are [used] in the sense of enmity; *duh* is remembered [as used] when there is no affection.
Indeed, "milking" (*dohana*) is cited as an example of "filling up" (*prapūraṇa*). ||2||
Likewise, *diha* is taught in the sense of accumulation, and *liha* in the sense of tasting; *cakṣiṅ* is used for manifest speech. These five, beginning with *div*, are without the augment *iṭ*. (3)

Furthermore, *cakṣiṅ* would have the anubandha *anudātta* in the sense of seeing; *pṛc* would mean "to be joined"; *pañcadaśa* would mean "there should be fifteen"; and *ras* would mean "motion" and "trembling. (4)
In this praise of Īśa, the wise have further explained that Īśa signifies sovereignty; moreover, *asa* is declared to mean "seating," while *śāsura* joined with *aṅ* signifies "desire. (5)
The root *vas* is said to mean "covering" (*ācchādana*), while *kas* means "motion" (*gati*) and "injunction" (*śāsana*).
Some, however, say that it is not *aniṭ*; yet even when it is *śānta*, it is treated as *aniṭ*. (6)

"The letter *ṇ* should be used for the act of kissing; this [letter] ends with the dentals and is the last of the palatals"—thus says the author of the *Ābharaṇa*, but this is considered an error. (7)
The letter *ś* is traditionally taught to occur in the pure (*śuddha*) and unmanifest (*avyakta*) sounds, as well as in the sound *chi*; the letter *j* is likewise remembered [to occur in these].
Some maintain that it occurs in "worship" (*samarcana*), while others hold that it occurs in both places.
Some say that the [syllable] *a* is a constituent part (*avayava*) of the word *avyakta*; others say it is the word itself.
The root *pṛjī* occurs when one is excluded from a group; the root *vṛjī*, however, is preceded by labials. (9)
Some say this [root] is *id*, while others hold it to be *pṛc*; it is traditionally remembered as *samparjana*.
The root *sūj* occurs in the sense of the act of releasing living beings from the womb. 10.
The roots *śīṅ* (to sleep), *stu* (to praise), and the last ones [of the preceding group] are *ñit* roots that take the *parasmaipada* endings;
*yu* (in the sense of mixing and non-mixing), *ru* (in the sense of sound, injury, and motion). 11.
The root *vṛdh* with the suffix *sūtra* is used in the sense of praise; *sthuraniḍ* and *athaṇas* are also used in the sense of praising.
*Ṭukṣu* is used in the sense of sound and flowing forth; *ṣṇu* is used in the sense of covering. (12)
The root *ūrṇu* is used in the sense of covering; *tuṣ*, however, is used in the senses of impelling and sovereignty.
Impelling means permission; *ku* is used in the sense of sound; indeed, these two [roots] are without the augment *iṭ*. (13)
The roots *stuñ* (to praise) and *syat* (to decay) take *sun* as their substitute; *bruñ*, however, is used for clear speech. These two are aniṭ (lacking the iṭ augment).
Due to their *ñit* designation, they are eligible for both padas (voices), yet *iṅ* (to study) is exclusively parasmaipada (active voice).
Excluding the suffixes beginning with *ś* and ending with *su*, there are twenty-eight in number;
the prefix *adhi* is always intended [to signify] study (*adhyayana*) when followed by the root *i*. 15.
The root *smṛ* preceded by *adhi* is always considered to mean "to remember. The root *vīr* signifies going, pervading, beauty, procreation, battle, and eating. (16)
The root *pra-jan* signifies conception, while *as* is considered to mean throwing or casting away;
here, the vowel *ī* is regarded as a different verbal root which, through phonetic combination (*praśleṣa*), is understood as *stām*. ||17||
The root *yā* is used in the sense of reaching; likewise, *gati* (going) is used in the sense of movement as well as in indicating (*gandhana*).
*Gandhana* means hinting or pointing out. *Bhā* is used in the sense of shining or radiance, while *ṣṇā* is said here to mean purification. 18.
The root *śrā* signifies cooking; for it shares its middle portion with the roots ending in *d*.
*Drā* is used in the sense of loathing and going; *psā* occurs in the sense of eating; and *pā* is used in the sense of protecting. (19)
*rā* occurs in the sense of giving (*dāna*), *lā* in the sense of taking (*ādāna*); *syātām* and *abhāvi* occur in the sense of giving.
Candra says that *dā* and *lavane* occur in the sense of cutting (*chidra*), while *khyāḥ* occurs in the sense of narrating (*prakathana*). 20.

The author of the Nyāsa maintains that the root [mā] preceded by the prefix *sam-* is not employed; however, he holds that this root is intransitive when it means "to measure," though it may become transitive through the influence of a prefix. 21.
In another sense, this usage by the learned of a transitive verb from a root meaning "to measure" is appropriate, as in the phrase: "Someone measures his belly with his fist. ||22||
The word *pañca* (five), when used by the learned in the sense of censure (*paribhāṣaṇa*), is employed with the suffix *-anta*, and it certainly does not refer to a large number. ||23||
Thus say others; other wise men declare that there is no *jhi* suffix.
Verbal roots beginning with *iṇ* and ending with *vac* are considered to be *aniṭ* (without the *iṭ* augment). 24.
The root *vid* is declared to mean "knowledge," *as* is said to mean "existence," *bhu* to mean "purity," and *mṛj* would mean "cleansing.
*Rudir* occurs in the sense of shedding tears, and *ñiṣ* is cited in the sense of purification. (25)
The root *śvas* is used in the sense of breathing; *anaś* is used for eating and laughing;
*jāgṛ* is said to mean the destruction of sleep; and *daridrā* is recorded as meaning being in a state of poverty or misfortune.
Likewise, *kāsṛ* is used in the sense of shining; *śāsu* is used for commanding and instructing;
and *dīdhīṅ*, which begins with a nasal (*ṅit*), is said to signify both shining and playing. (27)

In the Chandas (Vedic literature), five roots are declared [to have the same meaning as 'iṅ']: evīṅ, tuvi, and veti; furthermore, there are three other roots here that have the same meaning and are parasmaipada (active voice). 28.
The *ṣaṣasasti* meter consists of sixty-six [mātrās] and is proclaimed as being used for the *vaśa* and *kānti* meters;
"desire" (*kānti*) and "repetition" (*iccha*)—this is the *gaṇa-sūtra* in this context. ||29||

It is traditionally recorded that the meaning [of the rule] is that the *yaṅluganta* (the form with the elision of *yaṅ*) should be understood as belonging to the *adādi* class; the term *hā* has been mentioned in the sense of removal, whereas *anuṅ* is accepted by the wise as being without the augment *iṭ*. (30)
Thus end the *ityādi* verbs;
now follow the *juhotyādi* verbs:
some maintain that the root *hṛ* is prescribed for both taking and eating, as well as for seizing.
In the Bhāṣya, it is stated that the word *dāna* also signifies "pleasing. ||1||
The meaning of "prekṣapa" is indeed "dhā" and "dhāre" regarding the oblations;
this is obtained from the inherent nature [of the words], and thus there are four [syllables] in sequence. ||2||
Now, the root *ñibhī* is cited as being parasmaipada in the sense of fear;
*hrī* is used for shame, and the root *pṛ* is further said to mean protection as well as filling.
Others, however, hold that this [root] ends in a short vowel; *ḍubhṛñ* is used in the senses of supporting and nourishing;
*maṅs* is used in the senses of measuring and sound; and *hṅ* is traditionally taught thereafter in the sense of motion. (4)
In the sense of giving up (ohāk), this [root] takes the *parasmaipada* endings;
whereas *ḍudāñ* is used in the sense of giving (*dāna*), while *ḍudhāñ* is used in the senses of holding (*dhāraṇa*) and also nourishing (*poṣaṇa*). ||5||
Then there is *svṛ* in the sense of winding; *ṇijir* is used for purification and nourishment;
*vijir* occurs in the sense of separation; and *viṣlṛ* is proclaimed in the sense of pervasion. (6)
Now, there are some roots ending in the letter *ga* which belong to the Vedic language and take the *parasmaipada* endings;
among them, *ghṛ* is used in the senses of flowing and shining, while *hṛ* is traditionally taught in the sense of acting with force.
The roots *gati* and *vṛṣi* are used in two senses; *ṛ* is also recorded in the sense of speech.
*Bhas* occurs in the senses of threatening and shining; *kir* is in the sense of knowing, and *tura* is in the sense of haste. ||8||

The root *dhiṣ* is used in the sense of sound and grain; *dhana* means wealth; and *jana* means birth. The roots beginning with *gā*, *sū*, and *hu*, and ending with *sar*, are verbal roots (*dhātavaḥ*). (9)
The roots *ciketi*, *jigāti*, and *syu* are also stated to be aniṭ (not taking the augment iṭ) after the letter *r*. ||10||
Thus end the roots beginning with *hu* (juhoty-ādayaḥ).
Now follow the roots beginning with *div*, which take the *parasmaipada* endings; there are twenty-five such roots ending with *jhr̥ṣ*.
In play, in the desire for victory, in legal proceedings, in gambling, and in praise. ||1||
The root *div* is traditionally taught to mean "to shine," "to go," and "to play";
*ṣivu* means "to weave" or "to extend a thread"; and *srivu* means "to move" and "to dry. (2)
The root *ṣṭhivu* is said to mean "spitting"; some do not recite this one here.
*Snuṣu* would be for "eating," while some declare it to mean "taking. (3)

The suffix *ṣṇasu* is considered to occur after the root *adṛś* in the sense of "not seeing," while *knasu* is used in the senses of "concealing" and "shining"; here, "concealing" (*hvaraṇa*) is understood as crookedness (*kauṭilya*). ||4||
The root *pluṣ* is used in the sense of burning (*vyuṣo dāhe*), while *nṛtī* is taught for the tossing of limbs (*gātravikṣepaṇe*).
