*Tras* is declared to mean agitation (*vega*), and *kuth* is considered to mean putrefaction (*pūtībhāve*). ||5||
The state of putrefaction is indeed foul odor; the root *puth* is said to mean injury. The root *guh* is declared to mean concealment, and *kṣip* means impelling. (6)
The root *puṣpa* is said to mean "blooming"; likewise, *stimati* and *ṣṭima* denote "stiffness.
*Ṣṭīc* is said to mean "becoming moist," while *vrīḍa* denotes both "incitement" and "shame. (7)
The roots *iṣ* (in the sense of "going"), *ṣaha*, and *ṣuha* are cited as having the meaning of "capacity" (*cakyartha*).
Capacity is said to mean "satisfaction. The roots *jṛṣ* and *jhṛṣ* function in the sense of "loss of vitality" (*vayohāni*). ||8||
The root *pūj* is used in the sense of liberating living beings from the womb;
*dūṅ* is used in the sense of distress; this [root] *dī* is declared to be intransitive in the sense of destruction. (9)
The root *ḍīṅ* is used for moving through the air; *mīṅ*, however, is used in the sense of harming.
Here, "harming" means the separation of life-breaths, while *rīṅ* is proclaimed to mean flowing. (10)

The root *pīṅ* is used in the sense of drinking, *māṅ* in the sense of measuring, and *īṅ* in the sense of motion; *prīṅ*, however, is transitive. It is used in the sense of affection (*prīti*). Now, these four are recorded as being conjugated in the *parasmaipada*. (11)
*Śo* is used in the sense of thinning; *cho*, however, in the sense of cutting; *ṣo* in the sense of ending; and *do* is declared to mean breaking.
The roots beginning with *dhī* are remembered as being without the augment *iṭ*. (12)
Now, fifteen verbs ending in the ātmanepada are stated in order:
*janī* (to be born) in the sense of manifestation, *dīpī* (to shine), and *vāpyāya* (to swell) in the sense of illumination here. 13.
The root *pūrī* means "to become full"; *tūrī* is used in the senses of "going" and "hurrying.
Both *dhūrī* and *gūrī* are proclaimed to mean "injury" and "going. (14)
The roots *ghūrī* and *jūrī* are proclaimed to signify injury and the loss of vitality;
*śūrī* is used for injury and paralysis, while *cūrī* is declared to mean burning. (15)

Or rather, the final sūtra is intended as "tapa aiśvarya"; it is recorded as having the meaning that he undergoes (bhajati) sovereignty in the sense of performing penance, employing either the ātmanepada suffix taṅ or the parasmaipada suffix śyan. ||16||

Some maintain that the word *ba* signifies the meaning "otherwise" (*anyathā*) in the context of the *parasmaipada*; others hold that the sound *va* is the initial constituent of the root *vṛ*. Therefore, being chosen [by him], she entered the hall of Rāma. (17)
Thus they say that the usage by Bhaṭṭi is based on that;
an alternative reading is proclaimed as "patet" through such a transposition.
The root *vṛ* is declared to mean "choosing," while *kliś* is recorded in the sense of "affliction."
*Kāśṛ* in the sense of shining, *vāśṛ* in the sense of sound—these two are marked with the svarita accent; then there are five more [roots]. (18)
The root *mṛṣ* is declared to be used in the sense of endurance (*titikṣā*); *śuc* is proclaimed in the sense of purification (*īśuci*).
*Klid* is used in the sense of becoming putrid (*pūtībhāva*), while *ṇah* is intended in the sense of binding (*bandhana*). 19.

The roots *rañj* (to color), *rāg* (to color), *athak* (to cry out), and *śap* (to curse)—which is aniṭ—along with *kāṇ* and others, these eleven also have anudātta (low-pitched) indicatory marks. ||20||
The root *pad* is used in the sense of "going," *khid* in the sense of "dejection," and *vid* is desired in the sense of "existence.
*Budh* occurs in the sense of "understanding," and *yudh* is cited in the sense of "combat. (21)
In this [section], six roots beginning with *pad* are stated to be root-initial (*anudātta*) and lacking the augment *iṭ*;
among them, the root *aṇ*, meaning "to breathe," ends in a dental. Thus they have declared. 22.
In the knowledge of the mind and in meditative concentration (samādhi), there occurs the restraint of the active mind;
therefore, concentration is said to be characterized by the absence of activity. ||23||
The root *sṛj* is used in the sense of emission; *liś* is intended in the sense of becoming small.
Furthermore, roots beginning with *man* and ending with *rāg* are aniṭ (lacking the *iṭ* augment), following the sequence of the *dyat* class.

Regarding this gaṇasūtra, "vṛddhau caiva rādho 'karmakāt" [the root *rādh* ending in a long vowel takes the *parasmaipada* endings when used intransitively], its meaning is thus remembered by the wise: ||25||
In this very context, the word "śabda" (the suffix) has its order inverted; it is prescribed after the root *rādh* only when it is intransitive (*akarmaka*).
Therefore, the example given is "vṛddhau" (in the case of growth). Thus [ends verse 26].
"I do not grieve that the son of the Sātvatī woman commits an offense against me"—in this context, the word *rādhyati* is intended to have the meaning "to offend" (*druhyati*). (27)
"Who could forgive one who repeatedly causes offense?"—in this context, the wise should indeed infer that the meaning refers to one who acts with malice. (28)
In the expression "the rice is being prepared" (rādhyaty odanaḥ), the meaning intended is "it is being cooked" (sidhyati).
And in the expression "he is concerned for Kṛṣṇa" (kṛṣṇāya rādhyati), the meaning is "he is reflecting upon fate" (daivaṃ cintayati). ||29||
This root *vyadh* is indeed recited in two groups: in the first group (*bhvādi*) and in the tenth group (*curādi*).
*Vyadh* occurs in the sense of piercing; *puṣ* in the sense of nourishing; and *śuṣ* in the sense of drying. (30)
The root *tu* is said to mean "pleasure," *duṣ* is taught in the sense of "transformation," and *śliṣ* occurs in the sense of "embracing";
here, these seven roots beginning with *rādh* are aniṭ (without the augment iṭ). ||31||
The term *śaka* is cited here in the sense of "endurance" (*marṣaṇa*);
for the meaning of its being "optionally applied" (*vibhāṣita*) is that it functions as both [parasmaipada and ātmanepada] in this context. (32)
The root *ṣvid* is used in the sense of the trickling of limbs; its flow is traditionally recorded as *tattudharma*.
Indeed, the author of the Nyāsa and others state that this [root] should be *ñīd*. ||33||
*Haradatta* and others say "no"; *krudh* is proclaimed in the sense of anger;
*kṣudh* in the sense of hunger; and *śudh* in the sense of purification and the act of cooking. (34)
The reading *ṣidhu* having been cited here is stated to be an error;
six roots beginning with *śak* are *aniṭ*, while others say that *śak* is *seṭ*. (35)
The root *radh* is used in the sense of accomplishment and injury; here, however, its accomplishment is said to be completion.
Then, *naś* is used in the sense of disappearance, and *tṛp* in the sense of gratification. (36)
In this context, *tarpaṇa* (satisfying), *tṛpti* (contentment), and *prīṇana* (pleasing) are proclaimed as synonyms.
*Harṣa* (joy) and *mohana* (delusion) are mentioned; here, *darpa* (arrogance) is considered a form of delusion.

In the sense of wishing to kill, *druh* is prescribed; delusion (*moha*) is said to be a state of mental confusion, where this confusion is a lack of discrimination. In the sense of vomiting, *ṣṇuh* is recorded. (38)
The root *ṣṇiha* is used in the sense of affection; here, the suffix *vṛt* indicates the completion of the roots beginning with *radh*.
The root *śamu* is said to mean tranquility, while *tam* is declared to mean longing. (39)
In this context, the root *dam* (to subdue) is proclaimed to be *upaśama* when followed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*).
Therefore, this [causative form] is transitive; it is traditionally held to be intransitive like the root *śam*. (40)
The root *śram* is considered to mean asceticism, weariness, and instability;
*kṣam* is said to mean endurance; and *klam* is proclaimed to mean exhaustion. 41.
The root *asu* is said to mean "to rejoice" and "to throw"; *yasu* is declared to mean "effort";
*jasu* would mean "liberation" and "decay"; and *tasu* is cited as meaning "to perish. (42)
Furthermore, the word *vasu* [is used] in the sense of "giver" (*dasu*) when it occurs in the *stambha* [section], while others [use it] in the sense of "cattle" (*baśādi*).
Although it is recited in the *vyuṣ* section regarding the "burning of the east," it still possesses distinct meanings. ||43||
Furthermore, it is recited as having the meaning of "limb" (aṅga), beginning with a labial and ending with a dental. ||44||
Some say that *vyuṣ* means "to dawn," while others have stated that this [root] is *vay*.
*Pluṣ* occurs in the senses of burning and impelling; *vis* is used in the sense of binding, and *kus* in the sense of binding. (45)
In the case of emission, it is called *busa*; in the case of fragmentation, it is termed *musa*;
in the case of transformation, it is called *masī*; and transformation (*pariṇāma*) is indeed a process of change (*vikriyā*). ||46||
Some say that *samī* means "agitated," while *luṭ* is said to mean "churning.
*Uca* is declared to mean "assemblage," and both *bhṛśu* and *bhraṃśu* mean "falling. (47)
The root *vṛś* is declared to mean falling down; *kṛś* is used in the sense of choosing (*varaṇa*) or making thin (*tanūkaraṇa*);
and *tṛṣ* is traditionally taught to signify thirst (*pipāsā*). 48.
The root *hṛṣ* is proclaimed to mean satisfaction; *ruṣ* and *riṣ* are both declared to mean injury;
*ḍip* is used in the sense of censure; *kup* in the sense of anger; and *gup* is remembered to denote agitation. (49)
Yu-pū-ru-pu-ru-śa are declared to be the deluders (vimohana).
Lubha is used in the sense of greed (gārdhya); for here, greed is proclaimed to be longing (ākāṅkṣā). ||50||
The root *kṣubh* is said to mean "to tremble"; *ṇabh* and *tubh* are used in the sense of "injury";
*klid* is said to mean "becoming moist"; and *ñimidā* is considered to mean "affection. (51)
The root *ñiṣvid* is proclaimed to mean "to release" through affection;
*ṛdh* means "growth," while *gṛdh* signifies "desire," and *vṛt* here denotes "action. (52)
The *vṛt* designation is intended to indicate the completion of both the *vuṣādi* and *divādi* groups;
indeed, the application of the *vṛt* suffix is traditionally held to be for the purpose of fulfilling the *vuṣādi* category. (53)
Others have declared that [the verse] beginning with "likewise it wanes" (tathā kṣīyate) is established in this way. ||54||
Thus end the *divādi* roots;
now follow the *svādi* roots:
the root *ṣuñ* is used in the sense of pressing, as well as bathing (*snānam*), immersing (*snapanam*), and crushing (*pīḍanam*).
And here, the term "pressing" (abhiṣava) refers specifically to the mixing of the liquor.
In this context of bathing, this root *ṣiñ* is intransitive; it is said to mean "binding.
The root *śiñ*, beginning with a palatal (*tālavya*), means "sharpening," while *ḍumiñ* is recorded as meaning "to cast. (2)

The root *ci* is said to mean "piling," *stṛ* is declared to mean "covering," and then *kṛ* [is used] for "harming. These seven, beginning with *su*, are proclaimed as being *aniṭ* (lacking the *iṭ* augment). ||3||
The root *vṛñ* is used in the sense of "choosing," and *dhūñ* in the sense of "shaking"; *dhūñ* is also accepted as having a long vowel [at its end].
This [root *dhū*], however, has a short vowel at its end, is without the augment *iṭ*, and is conjugated in the *parasmaipada*. (4)
There are nine [roots] there; the first is *ṭudu*, remembered as meaning "to afflict";
*hiṃs* is used for "going" and "growth"; and *pṛ* is proclaimed to mean "to fill. (5)
Others say that one should touch [the breath] during both the maintenance of joy and its fluctuation;
however, the Master has declared that fluctuation is indeed life itself. (6)
Some say that *smṛ* [is used] in the sense of remembering; others, the followers of the Vedic tradition (*chāndasa*), say that it means "to protect" and so forth.
Here, *āplṛ* is considered to mean "pervasion," *śaklṛ* "ability," and *rādha* "accomplishment. (7)

In the section on roots with established forms (*saṃsiddhi*), the first nine roots beginning with *du* are considered to have an indicatory letter *iṭ*. Now, these two roots, *aśū* (to pervade) and *ṣṭigh* (to strike), are *anudātta*-accented;
they belong to the class beginning with *agaṇ* and are considered to take the *parasmaipada* endings. (8)
The root *stiga* (with the prefix *ca*) signifies going; *cās* signifies leaping; *ṣagha* signifies injury;
and *ñi dhṛṣā* is proclaimed to signify audacity. ||9||
*Dambh* is declared to be *dambhana*; *dambhana* is said to mean deception (*dambha*).
Regarding the root *ṛdh*, some have stated that it means "growth" (*vṛddhi*) and "satisfaction" (*prīṇana*), while others have called it *tṛp*. (10)
In the section beginning with "chandasī" (Vedic usage), the governing rule is stated to extend up to the end of the section on "aga.
The root *aṅ* signifies pervasion (*vyāpti*), while *dagh* signifies both killing (*ghātana*) and protection (*pālana*). 11.

The root *cam* is used in the sense of eating; then there are *riṣ* and *rikṣi* in the sense of injury. *Ciri*, *jiri*, *dāśṛ*, and *dṛc*—these three, along with *rikṣi* and *dṛc*, are roots that do not take the augment *iṭ*. (12)

According to one view, the word "kṣi" is included even in the list of verbal roots (dhātu) because it occurs in the spoken language; others hold that "aj-ādi" (beginning with 'a-j') refers to the verbal roots, so as to include *vṛt* and others here for the sake of completion. (13)
Thus end the *svādi* roots; now follow the *tudādi* roots.
The root *tud*, meaning "to strike" or "to afflict," is declared to be svarita-accented, to take the suffix *an*, and to be among the six that lack the *iṭ* augment.
The root *ṇud* is declared to mean "impelling," while *diś* is used in the sense of "granting permission. (1)
In this context, *atisarjana* is declared to mean giving; *bhrasj* is proclaimed to mean cooking;
*kṣip* is said to mean impelling; and *kṛṣ* shall mean scratching or ploughing.
The root *pṛ* with the prefix *parasmai* is proclaimed here as having the meaning of "going.
The four roots beginning from this point—*juṣ* and so on—are used in the sense of "pleasure" and "service. (3)
The roots *ovij* (in the form *vije*) meaning "to tremble" and "to fear" are stated to be ātmanepada;
likewise, this root *olajj* (in the form *lajj*), preceded by *ut*, and also *rolajj*, are generally [ātmanepada]. 4.
Now, there shall be one hundred and ten roots here that take the *parasmaipada* endings.
The root *ovraścū* is declared to mean "cutting," while *vyaca* is considered to mean "deception. (5)
The root *uch* is said to mean "to dwell" or "to shine," while *ṛcchati* is celebrated as signifying "motion," "the dissolution of the senses," and "taking on a form. (6)
In the sense of agitation, there is *utkleśa*; however, here *pīḍā* (affliction) is intended by *utkleśa*.
*Jarja*, *carca*, and *jharjhata* are used in the sense of threatening and reproaching. (7)
*Tvac* is said to mean covering; *ṛc* is cited in the sense of praise;
*uṣṇih* denotes straightness; *ujjh* means abandonment as well as delusion. (8)
Lobha (greed) is said to be delusion, while īhā (striving) is the state of being agitated;
riph is considered to be present in censure, violence, taking, fighting, and boasting. 9.
Some say "rih" [is used]; "tṛpa" and "tṛmpha" are indeed proclaimed to mean satisfaction.
Here, the first [term] should end in the nominative case, and the second should end in the accusative case. (10)

The two ending in the accusative case (tup and tumph) are also [used] in the sense of harming; then there are *tup* and *tump*, as well as *tuph* and *tamph*, in the sense of harming; and *dṛp* and *dṛmph* in the sense of agitation. (11)

In this [list], the first [root] ends in the nominative case, while the others end in the accusative; *ṛph* and *karmph* mean "to injure," whereas *guph* and *gumph* here mean "to tie" or "to string. (12)
The roots *ubh* and *mbh* are used in the sense of filling; *śubh* and *śumbh* signify beauty;
*dṛbh* is for tying; and *cṛt* is traditionally taught to mean both injury and binding. (13)
The root *vidh* is recorded in the sense of "arranging," while *juḍ* and *nuḍ* are also recorded in the sense of "going.
Regarding these, some have stated that the first [of the three] ends in the fifth letter of the dental class (*tavarga*). (14)
Likewise, *mṛḍ* is used in the sense of "to comfort," while *pṛḍ*, *pṛṇ*, and *vṛṇ* are used in the sense of "to please.
Furthermore, *mṛṇati* is proclaimed to mean "to injure. (15)
The root *tuṇ* is used in the sense of crookedness; furthermore, it is said to denote an auspicious action.
*Muṇ* is used for a promise, while *kuṇ* likewise denotes sound as well as an instrument. 16.
The root *śun* denotes motion; *druṇ* has the senses of injury, motion, and crookedness;
*ghuṇ* and *ghūrṇ* denote whirling; while *ṣura* signifies brilliance, sovereignty, and purpose. (17)
*Kura* is used in the sense of sound and cutting; *kura* is for enveloping; *mura* is [used];
*kṣura* is said to mean scraping; and *ghura* denotes both the terrible and the sound of distress. (18)
Some say that *puraḥ* occurs in the sense of "going in front," while this [root] *vṛh* occurs in the sense of "raising up";
others have stated that it begins with a dental-labial and belongs to the *pa*-class (the fifth class). 19.
The roots *tṛhū*, *tṛhū*, and *tṛṃhū* are proclaimed to have the meaning of "injury";
*iṣ* is declared to mean "desire," while *miṣ* is said to mean "rivalry. (20)

The word *cala* is used in the sense of playing with dice (*kālaśśvetya-krīḍana*), in sesame oil (*tilasneha*), and in the sense of moving about (*vilasana*); however, it is also proclaimed to mean a garment (*vasana*). ||21||
The root *vilas* is recorded in the sense of casting off sleep and moving; it begins with a dental labial (*dantyoṣṭhyādi*).
This same root, when beginning with a labial (*oṣṭhyādi*), is said to mean splitting apart (*bhedana*). (22)
The suffix *syāṇ* is used in the sense of "thicket" (*gahana*); *hila* is said to be used in the sense of "state" (*bhāva*) and "instrument" (*karaṇa*).
*Śila* and *śila* are declared to be used in the sense of "gleaning" (*uñcha*); *mila*, however, is considered to be used in the sense of "joining" (*śleṣaṇa*). ||23||
The term *likha* is said to denote the arrangement of the eyes; *kuṭa* is declared to mean crookedness (*kauṭilya*);
*puṭa* is stated to signify joining together (*saṃśleṣaṇa*); and *kuc* is considered to mean contraction (*saṅkocana*). ||24||
The root *guj* is used in the sense of sound and protection; *guḍ* is remembered in the sense of reproach;
*ḍip* is known [in the sense of shining]; *chur* is declared [to mean] cutting; and *sphuṭ* is considered [to mean] blossoming. (25)
In the sense of crushing, it is *pramardana*; likewise, in the sense of throwing, it is *akṣepa*. In the sense of cutting, it is *truṭa*.
This [root] with the vikaraṇa suffix *vāśyan* becomes *tuṭa* in the sense of the act of quarreling. 26.
The roots *cuṭ* and *chuṭ* are used in the sense of cutting; *juḍ* is said to mean binding;
*kaḍ* means intoxication; and *luṭati* is declared to mean embracing or clinging. ||27||
The root *kṛḍ* occurs in the sense of density (*ghanatva*); furthermore, density is considered to be compactness (*sāndratā*).
The root *kuḍ* is used in the sense of childhood; *puṭa*, however, is used in the sense of casting away (*utsarga*); and *ghuṭati* belongs to the *stau* group (the sixth class). ||28||
The root *tuḍ* is used in the sense of striking or breaking; *bhaḍ* means breaking.
*Thuḍh* and *thuḍ* are for concealing; others say *khuḍ* and *chuḍ*. (29)
The roots *sphur* and *sphul* are used in the sense of "moving"; however, *sphur* is traditionally recorded in the sense of "throbbing.
Some authorities declare that *sphul* is also taught in the sense of "moving. 30.
Some read [the root] with the vowel *a* as an upadhā, and also as *sphara*.
These three—*spuḍ*, *cuḍ*, and *bruḍ*—are considered to mean "covering. (31)

Some wise ones say that *nimajjana* (immersion) is [the root] *kruḍ*, while others say it is *bhṛḍ*. Indeed, this [root] is considered *anudātta-ita* (having an indicatory vowel *i* with a low pitch) when used in the sense of lifting up a heavy object. 32.

In the *stavana*, there should be four [verses] beginning with "ṇū stu" ending in a long vowel, which are parasmaipada forms of the root *it*; for it is desired that they serve for the shaking of the yoke-pole (*dhūr-vidhūnana*). ||33||

The root *guh* is said to mean the voiding of excrement; *dhru* means movement and steadiness—these two are [roots] that do not take the augment *iṭ*. Furthermore, the reading *dhruv* is also accepted as an alternative. (34)

Regarding the root *kuṅ* in the sense of "sound," Kaiyaṭa and others state that it ends in a long vowel (*-ū*), while Nyāsakāra, Tāraka, and others maintain it ends in a short vowel (*-u*); this entry here is for the sake of completing the *kuṭādi* group. (35)
The root *pṛṅ* is generally used in the sense of "exertion" (*vyāyāma*), and it is usually stated by the learned to be preceded by the prefix *vi-*.
The root *mṛṅ*, meaning "to abandon life" (*prāṇatyāga*), consists of seven forms and is indeed conjugated in the *parasmaipada*. ||36||

The root *riph* is used in the senses of going and supporting; *dhī* is used in the sense of dwelling, and also in that of going; six roots beginning with *pṛṅ* are without the augment *iṭ*; and *sū* is said to mean impelling. (37)

The six roots *kṛ* (to scatter), *vikṣepa* (to throw), *nigaraṇa* (to swallow), *gṛdhu* (to desire), *dṛṅ* (to see), and *ādṛ* (to respect) with the prefix *ā*, as well as *dhṛ* (to stand) and *dṛś* (to see), are all *parasmaipada* (active-voice). ||38||
The root *pracch* is taught for the sense of "desire to know"; roots beginning with *vṛt* and *kir* are taught for the sense of "completion";
*sṛj* is taught for "emission," while *masj* is said to be used in the sense of "cleansing. (39)
The root *ruj* is stated to mean breaking; *bhuj* is said to mean bending;
*chup* means touching; *ru*, *śṛ*, and *riś* denote injury; and *liś* denotes going. 40.
*Spṛś* is used in the sense of touching; *ṛdṛkṅādyāḥ*, twelve [roots] in sequence, are [listed]; then *viccha* in the sense of going, and *viś* is cited in the sense of entering. (41)
The root *mṛś* is said to mean touching; touching is considered to be *āmarśana*.
The root *ṇud* means impelling, while *ṣadlṛ* is said to mean falling apart and going. (42)

Likewise, *avasādane* (in the sense of dejection) and *śadlṛ* (in the sense of falling away) are stated [as roots]; then there are five beginning with *viśad* ending in *iṭ*, which are marked with the svarita accent; and then six beginning with *ṣaṇ*. 43.
The roots *mil* (to meet), *mṛc* (to release), and *lup* (to cut) [are used];
*vid* (to find) is used in the sense of obtaining; and *lip* (to smear) is used in the sense of coating—this is the desired increase [of meaning]. (44)
The root *sic* (to sprinkle) is *aniṭ* (without an *iṭ* augment); the five roots beginning with *muc* are declared to be *aniṭ*.
According to the systems of Vyāghrabhūti and others, the root *vid* (to find) is declared to be *seṭ* (with an *iṭ* augment). ||45||
Now, there are three roots ending in -th, which are *parasmaipada*:
*kṛtī* (meaning cutting), *khid* (meaning dejection), and *piś*, which is said to be *aniṭ* (lacking the *iṭ* augment) and meaning a part. ||46||
The word "vṛt" is used to indicate the completion of both the *mudādi* (curādigaṇa) and the *tudādi* (tudādigaṇa) groups.
Thus end the *tudādyaḥ*; now begin the *rudhādyaḥ*: *rudhir* (to obstruct) is marked with *svarita* [accent]; nine roots beginning from this one [are *svaritet*].
And *irita* shall be [the root] *bhid*, which is cited as meaning "cleaving. ||1||
*Chid* is used in the sense of splitting; *ric* should be used in the sense of purging;
*vic* is said to mean separation; and *kṣud* is considered to mean crushing. (2)
The seven roots beginning with *rudh*, which are aniṭ in the sense of "joining" (*yuj*), have been fully described.
Then there is *ucchṛd* in the senses of gambling (*devana*), shining (*dīpti*), disregard (*anādara*), and injury (*hiṃsā*). ||3||
The root *utṛd* is said to mean "cutting" and also "encircling"; this one is conjugated in the *parasmaipada*.
Now, the root *indhī*, which ends in *ñī*, signifies "flaming" or "illumination. (4)
From the root *sar* onwards, there are three roots that take the ātmanepada endings;
*khid* is said to mean dejection, while *vid* is declared to mean deliberation—both of these are without the augment *iṭ*.
Now, there are twelve roots ending in the *parasmaipada* [voice], in their respective order:
*śiṣlṛ* is taught for the sense of distinguishing, and *piṣlṛ* is recorded for the sense of crushing. (6)
The root *bhañj* is said to mean "to crush" (*tvāmardane*), while *bhuj* means "to protect" (*pālane*) and "to eat" (*abhyavahāre*).
These four roots, beginning with *śiṣ*, are proclaimed to be without the augment *iṭ*. (7)
The root *tṛh* and *hiṃs* are used in the sense of injury; *undī* has the meaning of moistening.
*Adhāñjū* occurs in the senses of manifestation, smoothness, beauty, and also going. (8)
The root *tañc* is said to mean contraction; *ovjī* means movement and fear;
*vṛjī* has the sense of avoiding; and *pṛcī* has the meaning of mixing together. ||9||
The formation of this *vṛt* (grouping) here is for the purpose of indicating the completion of the group beginning with *rādhā*.

Thus end the *rudh*-class [roots]; now follow the *tan*-class [roots]. The root *tan* is used in the sense of "expansion"; there are seven roots beginning with this one, which are marked as *svarita* (circumflex-accented), in this sequence.
The root *kṣaṇ* is used in the sense of giving and also in the sense of harming; likewise, there is also the root *kṣiṇ*. ||1||
The root *ṛṇu* is used in the sense of going; *syada* is in the sense of flowing; *tṛṇu* is said to mean shining; and *ghṛṇu* is traditionally known [to mean shining].
Now, there are two roots with the anudātta accent: *vanu* is declared to mean begging. (2)
According to the opinion of Candra, this [root] *man* is used in the *parasmaipada* for the sense of "understanding";
however, the root *kṛñ* (with the augment *ḍu*) is used in the sense of "making" (*karaṇa*), and the mention of *aniṅ* marks the end of the *vṛt* group.
Thus end the roots beginning with *tan*;
now follow those beginning with *krī*: the root *ḍukrīñ* is declared to have "exchange" as its meaning and "substance" as its object.
The root *prīñ* is used in the sense of satisfying and also in the sense of delighting; *śrīñ* is used in the sense of cooking; and *mīñ*, however, is used in the sense of harming.
The roots *ṣiñ* (to bind), *athāpravam* (the group beginning with *ath*), *skuñ*, and *krīñ* and others are *aniṭ* (without the augment *i*) in this [section].
Furthermore, there is the tetrad consisting of *stanbhu*, *skunbhu*, *skanbhu*, and *ssku*. (2)
In the Sūtra, every [root] meaning "to obstruct" takes the *parasmaipada* endings;
the first and the third [roots] are proclaimed to mean "to support. (3)

"Mādhava says that [the root] *yuñ* is used in the sense of extracting in the second [conjugation], but in the fourth it is for restriction; however, it is proclaimed as *aniṭ* (lacking the *iṭ* augment) in the sense of binding. ||4||
The root *knūñ* is proclaimed to mean sound, injury, and blowing; *pūñ* is celebrated [in the sense of purifying];
*lūñ* is said to mean cutting; and *stṛñ* is employed in the sense of covering. (5)
The root *kṛñ* is used in the sense of injury, *vṛñ* in the sense of choosing, and *dhūñ* in the sense of shaking;
these are declared to be twenty-three roots ending with *badṛ*, listed in their proper order. (6)
The root *śrī* ending in *parasmaipada* occurs in the sense of injury;
then *pṛ* is [used] in the sense of protecting, and *vṛ* is said to be used in the sense of filling and choosing.
Some say that *bhṛ* is used in the sense of supporting; others say it is used in the sense of threatening, as it is said to be torn apart (*udīryate*).
Some also say it is used in the sense of supporting, while *mṛ* is proclaimed to mean injury (*hiṃsā*). (8)
The root *dṛ* is used in the sense of tearing apart; *sṛ*, however, is said to mean the loss of vitality.
Some say it is *jhṛ*, while others say *dhṛ*; furthermore, *nṛ* means leading, and then there is *kṛ*.
The root *mṛ* is used in the sense of injury; *gṛ* in the sense of sound; *jyā* in the sense of the wasting away of vitality;
*rī* is used in the sense of motion and hissing; and here, *vṛk* signifies the act of hissing. (10)
The root *lī* is used in the sense of "adhering," *vlī* in "covering," and *plī* in "motion";
however, some maintain that *vṛt* is intended here for the sake of completing the *lvādi* group, as it belongs to the *pvādi* group as well. (11)
The root *vṛñ* is used in the sense of choosing (*varaṇa*), and *bhṛñ* in the sense of supporting (*bharaṇa*); others, however, know this [latter] differently.
*Kṣī* is for harming (*hiṃsā*), while *jñā* is for awakening and making known (*avabodhana-bodhaka*). 12.
The root *bandh* is used in the sense of binding; roots ending in *vṛñ* and *bhṛñ* that lack an indicatory letter *ṇ* (aniṭ) are considered [to take *ap*].
The root *vṛṅ* occurs in the sense of gathering (*sambhaktau*), while *śranth* is used in the sense of great joy (*pratiharṣe*) and releasing (*vimocane*). 13.
From here, twenty-four roots are declared to be *parasmaipada*.
*Manth* is used in the sense of churning; *śranth* and *granth* are used in the sense of binding. (14)
*Kuntha* is said to mean "to crush" or "to press together," while others say it means "to afflict.
*Kutha*, Duriga says, means "to rub," whereas *mṛda* here means "to grind" or "to crush earth. (15)
The root *kṣud* is used in the sense of crushing and happiness; *kuṣ* in the sense of anger and extraction;
*kṣubh* in the sense of agitation; and *ṇabha* and *tubha* in the sense of injury. (16)
The root *kliś* is said to mean "to afflict," while *aś* is proclaimed to mean "eating."
Some have stated that here the syllable "u" is a constituent part of the verbal root, serving as the means of subsistence.
The word *iṣat* is declared to mean "slight" (*abhūkṣṇya*); its repetition is called *paunaḥpunyam*.
Alternatively, it may signify "excess" (*bhṛśārtha*). Furthermore, the root *viṣ* is desired [to be used] with the prefix *ni-* in the sense of separation (*viprayoga*). 18.
The root *pruṣ* and *pluṣ* are used in the sense of moistening; however, *puṣ* is used in the sense of filling.
*Muṣ* is used in the sense of nourishing and stealing; the suffix *khac* is prescribed after these roots in the sense of manifestation from what has already come into being. ||19||

The manifestation of reality here is held to be an origination that transcends [ordinary] birth; some say "this is vomited," while others hold that *ahi* signifies "enmity" (*heṭha*) and thus conveys the aforementioned meaning. (20)
In the case of *upādāna*, the suffix *ghañ* is prescribed; this [suffix] is intended to be *svarita*-accented.
The formation of *vṛt* is considered to indicate the completion of roots beginning with *ky* and *dhā*. 21.
Thus end the kry-ādi roots; now follow the cur-ādi roots: *cura* is used in the sense of stealing, *cita* in the sense of remembering, and *yatri* is considered to mean contraction.
In this context, regarding the word *sphuṭi*, there is an alternative reading (*pāṭhāntara*) meaning "laughter" (*parihāsa*); thus, it is *sphuṭiḥ*. ||1||
The root *lakṣ* is used in the sense of seeing and marking; *kudr̥ś* is used for speaking untruths.
Some say *kuḍ* is used [in that sense], while *laḍ* is recorded as being used for serving. (2)
The sound *i* is considered to be for the purpose of lubrication (*snehana*), while *laḍi* is intended for lifting up (*utkṣepaṇa*).
Regarding this, some say it is the vowel *o*, while others say it begins with the vowel *u*.
One authority has declared that *laja* denotes the warding off of water;
*pīḍa* is said to mean immersion; and *naṭa* is considered to mean trickling down. (4)
Nāṭya, however, is the absence of perspiration; the root *śrath* is said to denote effort.
Some say that *prasthāna* is used in this sense, while *bad* is considered to mean restraint. (5)
The moon (candra) is said to mean "to bind" (bandh), while *pṛ* means "to fill" (pūraṇa); *arja* is said to mean "strength" (bala).
*Pakṣa* is declared to mean "to breathe" (prāṇana), and *parigraha* is expressed as "acceptance" (parigraha). ||6||
*Varṇa* means powder; others say it means "impelling," and it is also said to mean "description.
*Pratha* is stated to mean "renown," while *pṛtha* is declared to mean "scattering. (7)
Some say that in the context of "path," *ṣamba* is intended;
others say *śamba* and *sāmba*, while *bhakṣa* is desired in the sense of eating. (8)
The root *kuṭṛ* is used in the sense of cutting, threatening, and filling;
*puṭṛ* in the sense of becoming small; and *cuṭṭ*, *avaṭṭ*, and *uṣṭṭ* in the sense of disregard. (9)
The root *luṇṭ* is used in the sense of stealing; *śvaṭha* and *śaṭha* mean lack of refinement (or crookedness) and also going;
some say *śvaṭhī* [is also used]; then *tuj* and *pij* are used in the senses of injury, giving, and strength. 10.
Furthermore, some have declared that *tuja* and *pija* mean "a dwelling";
others say *laja* and *luji* mean "motion," while *pisa* is recorded as meaning "to go. (11)
The roots *śāntv* and *sām* are said to be used in the sense of conciliation; *paribhāṣaṇa* (reproach) is also mentioned [as a meaning].
*Śvalka* and *valka* occur in the sense of affection (*snehana*); others hold that *ṣṇiha* and *sphuṭ* [are used in this sense]. 12.
The root *smi* with the prefix *ā-* denotes disrespect; others say that *ṣmiṅ* signifies disrespect.
*Śliṣ* means to embrace; *pathi* means to go; and *piccha* means to cut or hack. (13)

The root *chadi* is used in the senses of covering and giving; *śraṇa* is generally preceded by the prefix *vi-*; *taḍa* is said to mean striking; furthermore, there are three roots: *khaḍ*, *khaḍi*, and *kaḍī*. (14)
The root *kuḍi* is used in the sense of protecting (*rakṣaṇa*), while *guḍi* is used in the sense of surrounding (*veṣṭana*).
Some authorities maintain that *ima* means "to protect," whereas others have declared that it is *kuṭhi*. (15)
Some, however, say that *guḍi* is also used; *khuḍi* is said to mean "breaking," while *vaḍi* is declared to mean "dividing"; some have even stated that *vaḍi* alone [expresses this]. (16)
The root *caṇḍ* is used in the sense of being fierce; *caḍi* in the sense of joy; and *maḍi* is recorded as meaning ornamentation.
*Bhaḍi* is declared to mean auspiciousness, while *chardi* is said to mean vomiting. (17)
For the roots *pusta* and *busta* are proclaimed to signify respect and disrespect, respectively;
*cuda* is said to mean incitement, while *ṇakka*, *dhakk*, and *kakka* denote destruction. (18)
The words *cukk* and *cukkau* are used in the sense of distress; *kṣalaḥ* occurs in the sense of the act of cleansing.
*Talaḥ* is declared to mean excellence, while *tula* is said to denote measurement. (19)
The root *dula* is said to mean "throwing upwards"; *pula* is said to denote "greatness";
*cula* is said to mean "height" or "elevation"; and *mūla* is declared to mean "ascending. ||20||
The *kāla* [potion] is said to be used for causing distraction and for piercing;
the *snehana* is called *tila*, and the *bhṛta* is declared to be *acala*. (21)

The root *pāl* is used in the sense of protection; *lūṣ* is indeed for injury; *mān* is desired [in the sense of measuring]; *śulba* and *śūrpa* [are used] as well; and *cuṭ* is declared to be used in the sense of cutting. 22.
The root *piṭ* is said to mean "crushing," while *paḍi* is declared to mean "destruction.
Furthermore, *pasi* means "the clearing of a path" as well as "going. (23)
The root *śulka* is said to mean "touching excessively"; *capir* is proclaimed in the sense of "going";
*kṣapiḥ* is used for "patience"; and *kṣajiḥ* is declared to mean "living in hardship. (24)
In the sense of a path, *śvarta* and *śvabhra* are used; *sūtra* means a thread, and *jñapa* means to make known.
This [root √jñā] occurs in the sense of knowing and making known, with a short vowel before a suffix beginning with a consonant other than a nasal (aṅ) or a vowel (aci). ||25||
Pariveṣaṇa is said to be Yama, and pariveṣaṇam is also [Yama];
here it is declared as veṣṭana, neither bhojanā nor veṣṭanā.
*Parikalkana* is declared [to mean] deceit, while others say it means a small arrow;
some say it means secret conduct, and *bala* is considered to mean the act of breathing. (27)
The root *ci* occurs in the sense of piling up, but not others; *mi* is used in the sense of measuring, while *gaṇ* is used in the sense of counting.
*Ghaṭṭ* is used in the sense of moving, whereas *must* is desired in the sense of a collection. 28.
*Khaṭṭa* means concealment; *ṣaṭṭa*, *sphiṭṭa*, and *cubi*—these three mean injury; furthermore, *pūla* and *pūrṇa* mean a collection or heap. (29)
Others, however, say that *puṃs* is used in the sense of increasing;
*ṭaki* is used in the sense of binding; and *dhūsa* is desired in the sense of making beautiful. 30.

This [term] ends in a dental; others say it ends in a retroflex when followed by another [retroflex], and ends in a palatal at the end. Likewise, they say "kīṭa" (insect) is used here in the sense of contraction among the letters. 31.
The root *cūrṇ* means powder; *pūj* is said to mean worship, and *ark* is said to mean praise.
Some say that *tap* means heat, while *śuṭh* is desired in the sense of laziness. (32)
The root *śuṭhi* is declared to mean drying up; *jaḍa*, however, is considered to mean impelling.
*Gaja*, *mārja*, and *marca* are proclaimed to have the meaning of sound. (33)
The root *ghṛ* is said to mean "flowing forth," while some also say it means "draining.
The root *vac* is used in the sense of "expanding," whereas *tij* signifies "sharpening. (34)
The root *kṛ* is said to mean "to call out" (*saṃśabdana*), while *vardh* means "to cut" (*chedana*) as well as "to fill" (*pūraṇa*).
Some have declared that *kubi* means "to cover" (*ācchādana*), and others have stated it is simply *kubhi*. (35)
They say that *libi* and *tubī* denote "not seeing," while *ardane* means "injury.
When speech is manifest, *hlapaḥ* and *klapaḥ* are said by others [to denote that]. 36.
Others say that *hrapa* means "to cover"; *cuṭi* is considered to mean "cutting"; *ila* would mean "impelling"; and *mrakṣa* is cited as meaning "speaking unintelligibly. (37)
The root *lmeccha* is used in the sense of "unmanifest speech," while *brūsa* signifies "joy.
Furthermore, *barha* has the meaning of "injury," and *garja* as well as *garda* denote "sound. (38)
For they indeed recite here that *gardha* occurs in the sense of longing;
and the ancients have stated that *niketana* means a dwelling, while *gurda* is said to mean protection in the *jas* stem. (39)
Some say that *kecu* means liberation; *īḍ* is proclaimed in the sense of praise;
*jasu* is declared to mean injury; and *piḍi* is said to denote a collection. (40)
Some say that *ruṣ* [forms] *roṣe*, *ruṣaḥ*, and *ruṭ*; *ḍip* is considered [to mean] reproach;
*ṣṭūp* is said to mean height. Now follow those with low-pitched (anudātta) indicatory letters. 41.
Furthermore, *ākusma* is to be understood as "consciousness" (*cit*) in the sense of "collecting" (*saṃcetana*);
*dāmṛ* is used in the sense of "giving" (*dāna*), while *daṃśa* would mean "biting," and *disi* likewise means "biting. (42)
Some have declared that *dasa* means both "to bite" and "to see";
*ḍapa* and *ḍipa* are said to mean "to collect," and now that [root] is being explained. (43)
For the maintenance of a family, they say the word is *cāndra*; another [word for] family is *kuṭumba*.
For secret speech, the word is *mantri*, and likewise, for spying, it is *spaśa*. (44)
Furthermore, *saṃśleṣaṇe* (in the sense of joining) is *tarja*; *tarja* is also used here for threatening.
*Vasta* means scenting or marking; *viṣka* is said to mean injury or killing. (45)
Some say that *hiṣka* means "one," while *niṣka* denotes a measure of weight; *calala* is used in the sense of desire, and *syama* is employed in the sense of deliberation. 46.
The root *gur* is said to mean "to lift up," while both *śam* and *lakṣ* denote "observation.
The root *kuts* is used in the sense of "censuring," and *ava-kṣip* is said to mean "throwing down. (47)
Some say that *truṭ* is used in the sense of cutting; however, in this [text], *kuṭ* is used here.
*Gala* is declared to mean flowing forth, while *bhala* is recorded as meaning reproach. 48.
*Kūṭa* is used in the sense of non-payment; others say *avasādana* [is used in that sense]. *Kuṭṭa* is for tormenting, while *vañcu* is declared to mean deceiving. (49)
The "binding of power" (śaktibandhana) is declared to be the bull; that binding of power is his capacity for procreation, and it is indeed the connection with power. (50)
The root *mad* is used in the sense of satisfaction joined with thirst; *div* is used in the sense of warbling;
*gṛ* is said to mean knowledge; and likewise, *vid* is used in the sense of consciousness. (51)
And this [root *vid*] is recited in the fourfold group [of roots] in the senses of "dwelling" (*vivāsa*) and "narrating" (*ākhyāna*);
it occurs in the sense of "existence" (*sattā*) as *vidyate*, and in the sense of "investigation" (*vicāraṇa*) as *vetti* and *vinte*. (52)
The root *vid* takes the suffixes *śyan*, *luk*, and *śnā* in the sense of "attaining" (*prāpti*) respectively;
this [root] is proclaimed as being used for the paralysis of the mind (*manastambha*) and for loathing (*jugupsā*). (53)
Indeed, the *gaṇasūtra* "kusma-nāmno vā" is proclaimed here;
this root *kusma* signifies the act of smiling in a contemptuous manner. (54)
The word *carca* occurs in the sense of study; likewise, *bukka* is used for barking. From the prefix *upa*, the word *āviṣkāra* is formed, and it is considered to mean speaking. (55)
Likewise, the root *kaṇ* is said [to mean] closing the eyes even without a prefix;
*jabhi* occurs in the sense of destruction; *ṣūda* in the sense of flowing; and *jasu* in the sense of striking. (56)
The root *paś* is declared to mean "binding," while *stṛ* is celebrated in the sense of "sickness.
*Caṭ* and *sphuṭ* both signify "breaking," and *ghaṭ* is said to mean "joining together" (*saṅghāta*). ||57||
In the rule "hantyarthāśca," there is a *gaṇa*-sūtra for the root *div* in the sense of crushing;
*arj* occurs in the sense of acquisition, and *ghuṣ* is stated in the sense of making a sound. (58)
Liberation (mokṣa) is said to be at the end; "end" (avasāna) is called casting aside (kṣepa).
For the prefix *āṅ* denotes continuity (*sātatya*), while others say it denotes *ghuṣa* when joined with *āṅ*. (59)
The root *las* occurs in the sense of artistic skill; likewise, it occurs in the sense of ornamentation. Furthermore, *būṣ* means to adorn.
Now, *ghoṣa* is considered to mean "shooting" or "casting," as well as "sound. (60)
The root *arh* is declared to mean "worship," while *jñāni* is proclaimed in the sense of "union" (*yoga*).
*Bhaj* is said to mean "bestowing," and *śṛdh* is considered to mean "laughter. (61)
The suffix *ra* occurs in the sense of "disfigurement" (*nikāra*) and "adornment" (*upaskāra*), since *ra* follows when there is no tasting (*atāsvādane*).
Some know the root as *laga* and *ragha*, while others know it as *raga*. (62)
The root *añc* is said to signify distinction; *ligi* signifies wonder;
*mud* is declared to mean contact; and *tras* is intended to mean supporting. (63)
Some say that in the case of *grahaṇa*, the vowel *u* occurs; others say it occurs in the case of *vāraṇa*.
In the case of *uñcha* and *udhra*, the vowel *u* is intended here as an integral part of the verbal root.
Thus some say; others say "no. Now, *muc* may mean "releasing" or "delighting";
*vas* may mean "affection" as well as "taking away. (65)
In the case of cutting, the *cara* is prescribed; in the case of doubt, the *cyut* is mentioned. Some know it to be used for enduring and laughing, while others understand it as *cyusa*. 66.
Some know *bhuva* in the sense of "smearing"; others understand it as "making fragrant.
Others say it means "thinking," and in this very sense, the root *kṛp* would have the sense of "trading. (67)

The word "sakarmakāt" (from a transitive root) is the basis for the subsequent rule; the *gaṇasūtra* extending up to the root *spadi* constitutes the scope here for the application of the causative suffix *ṇic*.
They explain that [the suffix] *ṇic* has the sense of "causing to do" (*sambhāl-karma-kāraṇa*).
For when there is a swallowing (*grasa*), the fruit of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is expressed as "he causes to swallow" (*grāsayati*). ||69||
It should be understood that [the root] *puṣ* is clearly known to mean "in the act of" (*karmaṇi*);
it is declared to signify "nourishing" (*dhāraṇa*) and *dal* is said to mean "splitting" (*vidāraṇa*). (70)

The roots *paṭ* (to weave), *puṭ* (to fold), *luṭ* (to roll), *kuṭ* (to bend), *tuj* (to strike), *mij* (to purify), *pij* (to purify), *luj* (to break), *bhaj* (to divide), *lagh* (to hasten), *tras* (to fear), *pis* (to crush), *kus* (to sound), *daś* (to bite), *kuś* (to gather), and *ghaṭ* (to strive). ||71||
The roots ghaṭ-, bṛh-, barh-, balh-, gup-, dhīp-, āy-, st-, vic-, chīv-, yodhayati, lokṛ, locṛ, ṇad-, and kup- [are used in the sense of "to sound"]. ||72||
The roots *lup*, *tarka*, *vṛt*, and *vṛdh* are proclaimed to have the meaning of "speaking";
likewise, *ruṭ*, *raji*, *laji*, *raji*, *dasi*, *bhṛśi*, *ruśi*, and *rusi*. (73)
Śīka, naṭa, puṭapuṭī, ruci, laghi, raghī, aghi;
rahi, mahi, and then laḍi, staḍi, and nalayati—these end in *sa*. (74)
These too may have the same meanings as those occurring in the previous Daṇḍaka list;
furthermore, *āpyāyana* is explained [by some] as "to nourish," while *pūri* has the sense of "injury" like *ruj*. (75)

The root *ṣvada* is declared to mean "tasting," and some have said that *svāda* is its [past passive participle] form; or rather, from the root *ā-ḍṛṣ* onwards, all the verbal roots in this section end with *dhṛṣ*. (76)

These two roots, *yuji* and *praci*, which are included among the group of roots meaning "to obtain" (as in the sense that "the beautiful ones always obtain [them]"), are considered to have the meaning of "restraining. (77)
The root *arca* is said to mean "to worship"; *ṣaha* is declared to mean "to endure"; *īr* occurs in the sense of "reproach"; and *lī* signifies "liquefaction. (78)
The root *vṛj* is used in the sense of avoiding; *vṛñ*, however, is taught as having the meaning of covering.
*Jṛ* signifies the loss of vitality, and *ji* is that which causes to flow away. ||79||
The root *vi-śās* is prescribed in the sense of separating as well as joining;
the root *śās* is used when something is not suitable for all purposes, while the prefix *vi-* is considered to denote excellence. (80)
*Tapa* is used in the sense of burning, while *tṛpa* and *tṛpti* denote satisfaction; others say *sandīpana* [is used for heating].
*Chṛdīḥ* is said to mean causing to boil, as are *cṛpa*, *chṛpa*, and *dṛpa*. (81)
Some say that *syu* means "kindling"; *dṛbhī* is cited in the sense of fear; *dṛbha* is said to mean "weaving" (*sandarbha*); and *śrath* is declared to mean "liberation. (82)
Others say that *mī* is proclaimed in the sense of injury;
*granth* is declared to mean binding; *śīk* is considered to mean indignation;
and *cīk*, as well as *ard*, are stated to mean injury, and this [latter] is marked as *svarita*.
The root *arh* signifies "to injure" (*hisā*), while the root *sad* joined with the prefix *ā-* signifies "to worship" (*pūjā*). ||84||
The root *śundhati* is prescribed in the sense of cleansing;
*chadaḥ* is said to mean covering; and *juṣaḥ* would mean enjoyment. (85)
For "parikīrtana" is declared to mean either deliberation or injury;
others say it means "paritarpaṇa," for that is the act of complete satisfaction. 86.
The root *dhūñ* is used in the sense of shaking; *prīñ*, however, is proclaimed to mean satisfying.
*Śrantha* and *grantha* refer to composition, while *āplṛ* is said to mean obtaining. (87)
Some say this [root] *sāntv* is marked with the *svarita* accent; others hold that it exists for the purpose of providing confidence (*śraddhā*), and that its form would be long. (88)
Furthermore, some wise men say that the suffix *cana* is prescribed after a preposition (*upasarga*) when used with the word *śraddhā*, as well as in cases of derision. (89)
The root *vad* is intended to be *svarita*-accented in the sense of "sending a message";
some say it is *anudātta*, while in the sense of "speaking," it would be *vac*. (90)
The root *mā* is said to mean "worship" and is used in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) when meaning "attainment";
*garh* is declared to mean "censure," while *mārg* has the sense of "searching. (91)
The root *kaṭh* preceded by *ut-* is used in the sense of grief; likewise, *mṛj* is used in the sense of longing (*utkaṇṭhā*).
Furthermore, *mṛṣ* is proclaimed [to be used] in the sense of purification (*śauca*), ornamentation (*alaṅkāra*), and endurance (*titikṣā*). (92)
The root *svar* is used in the sense of sound, and *dhṛṣ* is recorded in the sense of daring;
now the roots ending in long vowels are described in order, beginning with *kath*. 93.

The word *katha* is used in the sense of a continuous discourse; *vara* is said to denote desire; *gaṇa* is stated to mean a number; and the knowledge thereof is the cause for [the application of] that number. (94)
The two roots *śaṭh* and *śvaṭh*, ending in *ṭha*, denote speaking in a deceitful manner;
some have stated that *paṭ* and *vaṭ*, ending in *ṭha*, denote a book. (95)
The verbal roots *rahas* (in the sense of abandonment) and *styāg* (in the sense of stopping) are proclaimed as having the designation *deva*;
some say that *pat* (in the sense of going) is either causative (*ṇijanta*) or ends in *ad*. 96.
The *paṣa* [prefix] following a non-prefix (anupasarga) is said to have the acute accent (*udātta*) when it denotes throwing;
*rac* is declared [to have this accent] in the sense of refining (*pratiyatna*); and *kala* [has it] in the sense of counting (*saṅkhyāna*) and going (*gati*). 97.
The word *parikalpanā* may denote anointing with unguents, as well as the act of preparing a hand;
here, *damabha* is considered to mean miserliness, while *maha* is said to signify honor. (98)
Sāra, kṛpa, and śratha are proclaimed as synonyms for weakness;
spṛhā denotes longing, while bhāma indicates anger; and stuti signifies praise. (99)
They know *kheṭa* in the third case-ending to mean "slander" (*paiśunya*) and "eating" (*bhakṣaṇa*); others say it is *khoṭa*, while *kṣoṭa* is proclaimed to mean "reproach" (*kṣepa*). (100)
In the context of anointing, *goma* is mentioned; in the context of play, it is proclaimed as *kumāra*; furthermore, in the context of character, it is said to be *upadhāraṇābodhaka*. 101.
*Upadhāraṇa* is used in the sense of practice and conciliation;
*vela* occurs in the instruction of time; they know *kāla* to be another verbal root [meaning "to throw"]. (102)
*Palpūla* is proclaimed for the meanings "to wash" and "to blow"; *vāta* for "ease" and "service," while others say it means "attainment through service. (103)
The word *gaveṣaḥ* is used in the sense of seeking (*mārgaṇa*) and is also proclaimed in the sense of service (*upasevā*).
*Vāsaḥ* is said to mean clothing (*ācchādana*), while *nivāsaḥ* refers to dwelling (*pṛthakkṛti*). (104)
The root *bhāj* is used in the sense of seeing and delighting; *sabhāj* is said to mean honoring.
*Bhāj* is intended in the sense of delighting and serving, while it is declared to mean abandoning in the sense of falling away. ||105||

Furthermore, *ūna* means "deficient" or "less"; *kūṭa* refers to a sound or a peak, and it is said by some to mean "torment" (*paritāpa*); *ayam* signifies "burning" (*paridāha*), as well as a convention (*saṅketa*) and a village (*grāma*). ||106||
*kuṇa*, *guṇa*, and these others are declared to have the sense of address;
*cāt* and *kūṭa* also have the same meaning, as another reading is accepted. (107)
*Keto* and *niketa* occur in the month of Śrāvaṇa during the invitation (*nimantraṇa*);
likewise, *kuṇa* and *guṇa* are declared here for the formal address (*āmantraṇa*). 108.

The root *cātket* (or *cātket*) means a peak; *kūṇ* means contraction; *mṛg* means seizing or searching; and *sten* means theft. These are considered to be ātmanepada roots when used without the prefix *ā*. 109.

The root *pad* means "to go"; *gṛha* means "house" as well as "seizing" or "searching"; *mṛga* means "deer"; *kuh* is used for "causing wonder"; and *śūra* and *vīra* signify "valour" and "courage. (110)
In this context, *sthūlayati* would be a word expressing nourishment; *artha* would mean a request, and *satra* refers to the act of continuous giving. (111)
*Garva* is celebrated as pride; *sūtra* is proclaimed as binding;
*mūtra* is said to mean urination; and *rūkṣa* is declared to mean harshness. (112)
Both banks serve as reminders of the completion of the task;
others hold that there should be a single vessel for the discharge [of the breath], while another is for the purpose of observation. 113.

Some have stated that when there is slackening [of the suffix], the form *kartṛ* becomes *karta*; furthermore, after a root beginning with a consonant, the suffix *iṣṭhan* is frequently applied in the sense of the suffix *tṛn*. (114)
"One performs that," "one describes that," and "one transgresses by means of that"—in these cases, the form of the verbal root [is used] following the indicator of the agent or the instrument. (115)

These five *gaṇa*-sūtras indeed have the sense of the verbal root with the causative suffix (*ṇic*): *baṣka* is considered to mean "seeing," *ākhyā* "naming," and *citra* "to make variegated" or "to wonder. (116)
Sometimes that [element] may appear as a marvelous sight;
furthermore, the element named "shoulder" (aṃsa) is proclaimed to exist in the state of conjunction. ||117||
The root *vaṭ* is said to mean "dividing," while *laj* means "making manifest.
Some, however, hold that *vaṭi* and *laji* signify "mixing," which conveys the sense of contact. (118)
The term *saṅgrāma*, having an anudātta indicatory letter (*anubandha*), is declared to mean battle;
*stoma* is said to mean praise; and *chidra* and *karṇa* denote piercing. (119)
Some say "karṇacchedana" means cutting off the ear; others say "karṇa" refers to a different metal.
"Anda" occurs when there is impairment of vision, or it may be used in the sense of withdrawal. 120.
Thus they say at the end: "Daṇḍa" is declared in the sense of inflicting punishment;
"Aṅka" is used for a footstep and also for a mark; and "Aṅga" is likewise explained. 121.
Sukha and duḥkha refer to pleasure and pain; rasa is proclaimed to mean enjoyment as well as affection; and vyaya is defined as the expenditure of wealth. ||122||
Form (rūpa) exists in the act of forming; for here, indeed, there is the perception of form. What is called "the act of forming" (rūpakriyā) is simply the making of form (rūpakṛti). ||123||
"Cheda is said to mean 'cutting in two,' while chada is said to mean 'concealing';
thus some here declare. However, [the root] labh would have the sense of 'impelling. (124)
In this context, *vraṇa* denotes a wound that causes the awareness of the crushing of a limb;
*varṇa* occurs in the sense of coloring or painting, as well as in the sense of expansion and in qualities such as those mentioned in the scriptures. (125)
This collection of group-sūtras (gaṇasūtra) here is extensive;
other verbal roots (dhātus) should also be understood here according to the principle of "diversity" (bāhulaka). 126.

The root *parṇ* is used in the sense of becoming green; *viṣk* is intended in the sense of seeing; *kṣap* should be understood in the sense of sending forth; and *vas* likewise in the sense of dwelling. 127.
The root *tutth* means "to cover" in the sense of awakening (*bodhi*); other verbal roots (*dhātu*) are to be understood in the same way.
The rule for the *gaṇa* is that the suffix *ṇiṅ* occurs after the root *aṅg* in the sense of "expelling. ||128||

The forms *śvetāśva*, *aśvatara*, *gāloḍita*, and *āhvāraka* are established by the elision of the suffixes *-aśva*, *-tara*, and *-etaka* when applied to the tail and other parts; this is indeed accomplished [by the rule].
These two [terms] should appear in the list of gaṇas at the end of the book for the sake of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*).

It should be understood that all verbal roots (dhātus) are likewise established here; they have been well-compacted into these verses and explained for the satisfaction of beginners. Thus ends the section on the *cur*-class (*curādayaḥ*).
Now, the *kaṇḍvādi* roots:
*kaṇḍūñ* is used in the sense of scratching the limbs; *mantu* is proclaimed to mean anger (*āgasi*).
Some say it means wrath (*roṣa*); Candra states that this root takes the suffix *ñi*. (1)
The root *pūj* is used for worship and sweetness; *mādhurya* is used for beauty and heat;
*as* and *sūñ* are said by some to be used for non-existence; furthermore, the *leṭ* and *loṭ* moods are used for sleep and thievery respectively. 2.
Some indeed declare that *pūrva* is used in the sense of "prior existence" and *dīpta* in the sense of "flaming";
likewise, *lelā* is used in the sense of "flaming," while *iras*, *cerajira*, and *añ* are used in the sense of "envy. (3)
The root *uṣ* occurs in the sense of dawn; *veda* would mean dream or portent;
*āśu* would be expressive of seizing; *medhāḥ* [is used] in censure; and the root *kuṣubhyati* [is used in that same sense]. ||4||
Others say that *nīcaḥ* means "a servant" and *magadhaḥ* means "in attendance";
meanwhile, *tantaḥ* and *pampasiḥ* are cited as meaning "suffering," as well as the act of causing such suffering. (5)
Furthermore, pleasure and pain are considered by the wise to be the highest [aim] in worship;
the word *ārā* occurs in the sense of action, while *arara* occurs in the sense of medical treatment. (6)
*Bhiṣakṣya* means "he will heal," while *bhiṣṇaj* is proclaimed in the sense of "serving.
*Iṣudhi* refers to "holding arrows," *caraṇa* means "going," and *varaṇa* means "protection" (or "choosing"). ||7||
*Curana* is said to mean theft; *turaṇa* is recorded as meaning haste;
*bhuraṇa* occurs in the senses of supporting and nourishing; and *gadgada* refers to that which is faltering. (8)
In the case of a slip of the tongue, *athasuri*, *elā*, *kelā*, and *khelā* are used by way of playful charm;
others say *ila* is also used, and *lekhā* may likewise be used for a faltering utterance. (9)

Others, however, maintain that this [root] is *ad* (to bite); for the root *liṭ* is used in the sense of slight reproach. The root *lāj* is declared to mean "living," while *hṛṇīṅ* signifies shame and anger.
The word *mahīṅ* is used for worship, praise, and also for accomplishment;
furthermore, *dravaḥ* is recorded as meaning affliction and service. (11)
*Tir* signifies disappearance; *agada* is considered to mean freedom from disease;
*uras* has the sense of strength; and *taraṇa* is said to denote movement.
*Payas* signifies a handful of water, and it is also intended to mean "having come together."
In abundance, in nourishment, in restraint, and indeed in the sky. ||13||

The *kaṇḍvādi* group is a class of words defined by their form, characterized by fifty [roots]. By that [group], *samar-* is used in the sense of battle, and *lāṭ-* is said to be used in the sense of seizing. (14)
*Velā* occurs in the sense of a boundary; *mṛga* signifies salutation and worship;
*jana* means searching, and likewise signifies affliction. (15)
This includes [roots] such as *paricary* and *arthak*.
Here, all [roots] ending in *ñ* or *ṅ* that take the *ātmanepada* suffixes are considered to be *parasmaipada* [in this context]. (16)
Thus end the *kaṇḍvādi* roots.
Verbal roots are indeed of two kinds: accented (*udātta*) and unaccented (*anudātta*).
Here, the augment *iṭ* shall be applied to an *ārthadhātuka* suffix beginning with a consonant (*val*) after those roots that have an acute accent.
Since that [list] would not suffice for those roots that are not udātta, those roots are here described in order according to the ancient *kārikās* as they were recited by them. 2.
The roots with initial *u* and *ṛ*, those ending in *y*, *t*, *ṛ*, *kṣṇu*, *śīṅ*, *ṣṇu*, *ṇu*, *kṣu*, *śvi*, *ḍīṅ*, and *śri*;
as well as *vṛṅ* and *vṛñ*—these, excluding the single-vowel roots, are recorded as being *nihata* (marked with a grave accent) among those ending in vowels. ||3||

The roots śaklṛ (to be able), muc (to release), ric (to leave), vac (to speak), vic (to separate), vic (to enter), siñ (to sprinkle), prachchh (to ask), tyaj (to abandon), nijir (to purify), bhaj (to share), bhañj (to break), bhuj (to bend), bhrasj (to fry), masj (to bathe), yaj (to sacrifice), yuj (to join), ruj (to break), rañj (to color), vijir (to tremble), svañj (to embrace), sañj (to cling), and suj (to press)—these [are the roots ending in consonants]. ||4||

The roots *ad*, *kṣud*, *khid*, *chid*, *tudi*, *nuda*, *padya*, *bhid*, *vid* (vidyati), *rvinid*, *śad*, *sadī*, *svidyati*, *skandi*, *hadī*, *krudh*, *kṣudhi*, and *budhyati* [are used with the genitive]. ||5||
In battle, bind, obstruct, accomplish, pierce, purify, succeed, and be perfected. ||6||
The roots *manya*, *han*, *āp*, *kṣip*, *chupi*, *tap*, *tipa*, *stṛpyati*, *dṛpyati*;
*lip*, *lup*, *vap*, *śap*, *svap*, *sṛpi*, *yabh*, *rabh*, *labh*, *gam*, *nam*, *yami*, *rami*;
*kruśi*, *rdaṃśi*, *diśī*, *dṛś*, *mṛś*, *riś*, *ruś*, *liś*, *viś*, *spṛśaḥ*, and *kṛṣi* [are included]. (7)
The roots *tviṣ*, *tuṣ*, *dviṣ*, *duṣ*, *puṣya*, *piṣ*, *viṣ*, *śiṣ*, *śuṣ*, and *śliṣ*—these end in *yat*;
likewise, *ghas*, *vas*, *dah*, *dihi*, *duh*, *nal*, *mil*, *rul*, *lil*, and *vah*. (8)
Among the roots ending in consonants, one hundred and two have anudātta (low-pitched) accents;
they are, in order: ka, ca, cha, ja, jha, da, dha, na, pa, bha, ma, śa, ṣa, sa, and ha. (9)
*Kacakāṇaṇaṭāḥ*, *khaṇḍo*, *gaghañāṣṭakhajāḥ* are recorded; those two which exist in the *tudadi* class according to one opinion are [also] found in the *curadi* class. (10)

The designation *śyan* is employed for the roots *tṛp* and *dṛp* in order to exclude [the suffixes] *vā* and *ra*. Furthermore, *svidy*, *pad*, *sidh*, *budh*, *man*, *puṣ*, and *śliṣ* take the suffix *śyan*. (11)
The suffixes *vasi*, *śa*, and *pāluk* are specified for the purpose of excluding others; likewise, these roots—*ṇijir*, *vijir*, and *śaklṛ*—are accompanied by indicatory letters (*anubandha*). (12)
Candragomin and others know [this rule], and it is seen as desired even in the Bhāṣya; however, it is established that Vyāghrabhūti and others did not include it here. 13.

The roots *rañj*, *masj*, *adi*, *pad*, *tud*, *kṣudh*, *śuṣ*, *puṣ*, and *śiṣ*—these are either not mentioned in the Bhāṣya or are mentioned here [by us], according to the consensus of Vyāghrabhūti and others. (14)
Thus ends the Dhātukārikā.
